title: Hold to snap and say what's in it
short: Log a meal with one press: the photo is taken the moment you press, and you say what's in it while you hold. Let go and both go together.
body: Chris, on build 244, after Basil misread a photo of his food: "a picture alone is not good enough. I have to mention how much butter is in it or did I use copious amounts of cooking oil?" Now + has Snap and say. The camera fills the screen with one big button. Press it and the photo is taken right then; keep holding and the mic listens, with the waveform and your words showing over the picture. Let go and the photo and the words go to the agent as one message, so Basil reads "two eggs in a lot of butter" with the picture and counts the butter. Slide left to the trash to throw both away, like hold to talk. Agents can ask for it too (camera "Snap your plate" +say), and a drawer shortcut can open it straight away (url=yui://snap), which Basil's Log a meal shortcut will use. Words are turned into text on the phone; only the text and the photo are sent. Tests: the new hold, let go and trash UI tests, the deep link and shortcut unit tests, the native runtime and the Hermes plugin both getting the words and the photo in one turn. Reaches phones with the next TestFlight build.

Holding the button: the photo is frozen, a coral waveform and the words Two eggs in a lot of butter show over it, and a trash button waits on the left.
Basil answers on the full screen: Two eggs, and the butter counts, with a Breakfast card of about 250 kcal, most of the fat from the butter.
Basil's thread: the eggs photo and the caption Two eggs in a lot of butter as one message, with Basil's reply under it.

title: Every agent keeps its own little database
short: Your agents now keep their own tables. Say add milk to my groceries or log today's bench and it lands in a table you can see.
body: Chris: "Make sure they have the ability to spin up little dbs of their own. They have their own tables. They have great starter values and can be a personal assistant for many tasks." Now every starter agent keeps its own small database, one per person and per agent, on the server. It writes with the same Agent tables words the spec and the playground already use (table, put, query), and every answer is drawn as a table, list, chart or stat with the real rows, never raw data. Each agent starts with tables worth having: Yui has to-dos, groceries and notes. Basil has 44 common foods with calories and macros per portion, plus meals. Arnold has 16 exercises with how-to cues, this week's plan and sessions. Penny has tasks, errands and bills due, Quill a first deck and its review queue, Gouda saved loops and songs. The blank agent makes its own. Ask for a new one ("make me a table for my reading list") and it appears. Totals by day, week or month work too. Deleting never happens on the agent's say: you get a Delete or Keep button and only your tap removes anything. Controls list each agent's tables with their row counts. Tests: runtime 121 of 121, the migrations on a local Postgres first, the four table asks three runs in a row at 54 of 54, and a full walk on a throwaway account in the simulator, light and dark, deleted after. No new app build needed: today's app draws it.

Basil answers What did I eat this week? with a list of three logged meals and their calories and macros.

title: Yui 0.4.3: swipe back, and a new install starts at Sign in
short: Build 258 is on TestFlight. Swipe sideways on the full screen again, and a fresh install opens at Sign in.
body: Build 258 is Yui 0.4.3, a small build with two fixes from beta feedback on build 244. Swipe works on the full screen again: drag right for the drawer, drag left for your other screens, and the plus, T and mic stay at the bottom of every screen. And installing Yui again no longer opens signed in to the last account: a new install starts at Sign in. Nothing else rides this build. The memory check passed before upload: no new leaks, 2.4 MB of growth over three rounds, a peak of 205 MB.

title: Every crew agent says what it does
short: Each starter agent now has a line under its name, two sentences on what it does and three things to ask it. And its hello is an answer, not something waiting in Review.
body: Chris on build 244: "I have no idea what this agent even does." Every starter profile (Yui, Arnold, Basil, Gouda, Penny, Quill and the blank one) now carries a `tagline` under 8 words, an `about` of two short sentences and `can`, three things to ask it. Basil's reads "Eat better without counting everything". The agents list sends them with the crew offer and on every crew agent's row, so Add agent, the picker and About can show them (the app screens are YUI-167); older builds ignore them. When Yui makes a new agent, or a blank one sets itself up, it writes its own. Second fix: Gouda's first pick sat in the drawer's Review tab as "1 thing is waiting on you". Review counted every unanswered question in the thread, the hello included. Now the first message is marked as the hello and Review skips it; later questions still count. Gouda's first beat also sits on the backbone now, kick on 1 and 3 and snare on 2 and 4. Tests: runtime 105 of 105, app unit 242 of 242, the drawer and first-launch UI tests, and the live crew check 19 of 19 on a throwaway account. The app half ships with the next TestFlight build.

title: Every agent has its own home: the spec and a mock
body: Beta feedback on build 244: "When I go to one of these agent screens, I should see a unique set of shortcuts." And for Gouda: "When I scroll the other way I should get the looper, the chord machine, and maybe some type of piano to jam along." This is step one, a spec and a mock you can tap, before any app code. Open an agent and its home shows two to four big shortcuts above the bar, and anything waiting on you right there, not only in the drawer. Swipe left for its starter screens, ready from the first open: Arnold's week and today's workout, Basil's calories and grocery list, Gouda's looper, chords and keys. No new Yui Lines word: shortcuts are the menu shortcut lines agents already send, and starter screens are pages 2 and up, so any agent can set its own home. Native agents get a home.yui in their profile. Not built yet: try it at /mockups/home.

title: The chat on this site feels like Yui
short: Open the chat and the site goes dark, Yui takes the stage, and she answers with screens you can tap: a beat, a chart, the crew.
body: The bubble at the bottom right used to answer in plain text. Now it works like the app. Opening it turns the whole site dark, the same switch as the moon button, and closing it puts back whatever you had. Nothing about it is saved past your visit. On a phone the chat takes the whole screen, like the app's stage; on a computer it is a tall panel. Answers play in: the first line in big type, then the screen. Yui draws with the site's own renderer, so a reply can be a choice, a list, a chart, a timer, a deck, a map, a game or a loop that plays. Tap a button and your tap goes back to her, and she builds the next screen. She follows the same rules as the channel guide the app's agents get: screens, not paragraphs, one idea at a time, no dashes. Four starters open the chat (What is Yui?, Show me a screen, Meet the crew, Make me a beat) plus a real button to get Yui on TestFlight. Meet the crew lets you tap Arnold, Basil, Gouda, Penny or Quill and see a screen each one would draw. The limits stay: a set number of turns per chat and per visitor, and a check for a person once its keys are in. No photos, video or outside links can be drawn here.

title: Swipe sideways on the full screen again
short: Drag right on the full screen for the drawer, drag left for your other screens. The plus, T and mic stay on every screen.
body: Chris, Sep 27, on build 244: "On the screen we lost the left and right scroll functionality." When answers moved to the full screen, the sideways drag stayed behind in the chat. Now a drag left on the full screen shows the next screen, a drag right the one before, and on the first one a drag right pulls the drawer out with your finger, the same as in the chat. It works on the empty greeting too. The plus, T and mic sit under every screen. A new test swipes both ways in light and dark and fails on the old build; the first run, screens and top bar tests still pass. It rides the next TestFlight upload. Per-agent home screens with a log-food shortcut and notifications up front are the next step, placed on the roadmap.

title: Agents answer on a screen, not in markdown
short: Ask any starter agent what it can do and you get one line, a list and buttons, not bullets cut into eight pages.
body: Beta feedback, Sep 27: asked Basil "What are some of the things that you can do for me?" and got a wall of markdown. The phone showed the stars around each bold word, ran the bullets together and cut it into 8 pages to swipe through. The live check of the starter crew never caught it: it asked each agent only about its own job, never an open question, and it did not look for markdown. Now it asks all six "What can you do for me?", "Tell me about yourself" and a breakfast's macros, and fails an answer with markdown, more than about 50 words of chat or more than 4 pages to read. On the old runtime those asks failed on every agent. The fix is on the server, no app update. The rules every native agent reads now say one line first, then a screen: what it does as a list and where to start as buttons, numbers as one table. Behind that the runtime cleans up what a model still gets wrong: bullets, headings and bold become a list and lines, short pages are merged down to 4, a run of number tiles (each tile played as its own page) becomes one table, and a table row or title written the wrong way is mended. Two bugs the new asks turned up are fixed too: a message sent while another agent was handing you over could go unanswered, and a list or step inside a deck broke the whole screen. Of the last six runs of all 392 checks, three came back clean and the others missed one to five, mostly an answer a few words over the limit.

After: one line, I'm your nutritionist, then a What I do list of five things and Where to start buttons: Plan my meals, Read my plate, Build a grocery list

title: Several chats with one agent: the spec and a mock
body: Beta feedback on build 244: "I think we might need to introduce the concept of multiple chats. Those should go in the left side bar." This is step one, a spec and a mock you can tap, before any app code. A chat is one conversation with one agent. New chat opens an empty one, saved only once you say something, and your first ask becomes its title. The drawer's Home now puts chats first, newest on top, with Next up and your pinned screens below. Hold a chat to rename or delete it, and delete asks first. Screens, the shelf and memory belong to the agent, so a new chat still knows you and your pinned screens are the same in every chat. The spec also sets out the database and host changes for step two: one new table, a chat id on each message, and one session per chat on the host. Not built yet: try the mock at /mockups/chats.

title: The starter crew stays in character
short: Arnold and Basil ask about injuries, conditions and allergies before a plan, and no crew answer ever comes back empty.
body: Every new person starts with six agents: Yui, Arnold the trainer, Basil the nutritionist, Gouda the musician, Penny the planner and Quill the study buddy. Now there is a live check that each one stays itself. It makes a throwaway account, confirms all six are there and each opens with its own first answer, then asks every agent two things on the hosted runtime and scores all 18 answers: the right job and the right screens, Yui Lines that parse instead of a wall of text, no dashes, no stray line breaks. Arnold and Basil are careful coaches, so they get stricter checks: ask about injuries, conditions and allergies before a plan, one short doctor note in the first answer, never a diagnosis, never an insulin dose. The first runs caught real problems. Basil's hello had no doctor note and never asked about conditions. Asked for a dose, he said to check with a doctor twice and gave no screen. Gouda sometimes wrote an answer the runtime stripped to nothing, and the turn closed with no reply. The fixes went live on the server, no app update: sharper rules for the coaches and Quill, a runtime that asks the model again when an answer has nothing to see and says so if it still can't, and small repairs for options that wrap onto their own line. The last three full runs passed all 164 checks, 29 of 29 for Arnold and Basil each. Test accounts were deleted after every run.

title: A new install starts at Sign in
short: Installing Yui again opened signed in to the last account, top bar and all. Now it starts at Sign in.
body: Beta feedback, Sep 27: "I just downloaded this app for the first time and I already see a header like I'm logged in." He had not signed in. The phone's keychain keeps an app's saved login even after the app is deleted, so the new install found the old session and skipped Sign in, 11 seconds after opening. The first launch of an install now forgets any login an earlier install left behind, so the first screen is the wordmark and Sign in with Apple, with no menu, agent picker or full screen button. An update from an earlier build keeps you signed in. A new UI test fails on the old code and passes now: a reinstall and signed out show no top bar, signed in shows it as before. Rides the next build.

title: Line breaks read as lines
short: Native agents wrote \n to break a line and the app showed the letter n. Now a list reads as a list.
body:
Basil answered a dinner question with one long say line and 
 between the dinners. In Yui Lines a backslash only escapes the next character, so the app showed 'allergies:nn• Grilled chicken...greensn• Salmon'. Two fixes on the server, no app update. The native runtime now tells the model that one line is one line: a new line is a new say, and items are one list line. And every answer gets one more sweep before it is written: a say with 
 breaks becomes one say per line, a run of bullets becomes a list, and a break in any other quoted string becomes a space. Live, three dinner asks on throwaway accounts came back as clean list and choose lines, with no 
 left. Hosted agents on Opus did not do it in the channel eval, and GLM 5.2 on the guide alone skipped it in 4 of 4 runs; the new eval case (list-no-escaped-breaks) catches it on the original reply and passes it after the sweep.

After: the same answer as a line, a list of five dinners, and a question

title: Add agent, then Cancel, no longer crashes
short: Opening Add agent and backing out crashed build 229. The chat screen is lighter now and it stays up.
body: Beta feedback, Sep 27: "I tried to add an agent and then I canceled and it crashed." The crash was not in Add agent. When the sheet closed, the chat screen redrew, and the phone had to spell out the chat's full type to do it. That type was nested 129 levels deep, and spelling it out ran the phone's small main stack dry inside the message bar. The simulator never showed it: its main stack is eight times bigger. The chat's layers, the thread and the message bar are now boxed up as separate pieces, so the deepest part is 47 levels. Nothing on screen changed. A new test keeps the chat's type under 60, and a UI test opens and cancels Add agent twice, with stage first on and off, and checks the app is still up. Rides the next build.

title: Long asks always get an answer
short: Hosted Yui used to think through a long ask and say nothing. Now she answers every time.
body: Ask hosted Yui to explain the rise and fall of Rome and, some of the time, you got nothing back, or a line saying she ran out of room. The channel eval found why: GLM 5.2, the model behind native Yui, could spend all 2000 tokens thinking and never start the answer. Two fixes on the server, no app update. Thinking now gets its own 1000 tokens on top of the answer's 2000. GLM treats that as a hint, so when an answer still comes back empty, or cut off after the model spent most of its room thinking, the runtime asks once more with thinking off and sends that answer. On the three eval cases that used to come back empty, 18 fresh turns gave 18 answers. Live, the same Rome question on a throwaway account came back as a 4-page deck with a map of the empire at its peak, a chart and the chain of failures, in 7 to 25 seconds.

images.alt: Before: hosted Yui says 'Yui ran out of room before it could answer. Try a shorter message.'
After: the live answer, a 4-page deck 'Rise and fall of Rome' opening on a map of the empire in 117 AD

title: No dashes in the crew's replies
short: Hosted Yui and the crew write like the house voice now: a period or a comma, never an em dash.
body: The first live proof of hosted Yui caught a small thing that mattered: she answered 'Arnold's your trainer — tap Arnold', and Arnold's hello had one too. The house voice has no em dashes. Two changes on the server fixed it. Every native agent's rules now say to use a period, a comma or a colon instead. Models still slip, so the runtime sweeps each answer once more before it is written: a spaced dash becomes a period when a new sentence starts after it and a comma when it does not, number ranges get a plain hyphen, and only the words a person reads are touched, never links or the inside of a screen's tokens. It went live without an app update. The proof is the same throwaway-account run on a fresh iPhone simulator: Get fit, and Yui now says 'Arnold is your trainer. Tap Arnold in your crew', with no dash in any of the seven crew answers on the account. The account was deleted after.

title: Native Yui on your phone
short: Build 229 is on TestFlight. Sign in and Yui talks first, the crew is already there, and Basil reads a photo of your plate.
body: Build 229 is the native sprint in one TestFlight build. A brand-new account signs in and Yui talks first, with Arnold, Basil, Gouda, Penny and Quill already in the list. Nothing to pair and nothing running on your own computer. The recording is a throwaway account on a fresh iPhone simulator against the live backend, start to finish: Yui's hello, a question to Arnold that comes back as a timer and a checklist, then a photo of lunch sent to Basil, who answers with a calorie guess, protein, carbs and fat, and a form to fix it before he saves it. Recording it caught a real bug: the phone sent the photo under one name and the hosted agent looked for another, so Basil answered a salmon plate with 'snap a photo'. The fix was on the server, so it reached build 229 without a new upload. Web search is in the build but waits on its search key, so it says it could not look something up for now. The test account was deleted after.

title: Everyone gets a Yui at sign-in
short: A brand-new account signs in and Yui is already there, hosted, and she answers. Nothing to pair, nothing running on your own computer.
body: This is the moment the native sprint was for. We made a throwaway account on the live backend, signed it in on a fresh iPhone simulator and did nothing else. The app opened in Yui's thread with her first message and the whole crew already in the list. We tapped Get fit and Yui answered for real: the tap went into the database, a webhook woke the hosted runtime, and her reply came back on screen in a few seconds. Arnold said hello on his own a moment later. No pairing code, no Hermes, no computer. Behind it, every person gets one hosted connector and native agent rows the first time the app lists their agents, and people who already had agents get the crew too, placed above their own with nothing replaced. There is one switch for all of it: with native_enabled off a new account gets no crew and a message wakes nothing, and switched back on Yui answers again. Both checks are now live tests in the repo, and the test accounts were deleted after.

title: How well GLM uses Yui
short: Native Yui runs on GLM, so both GLM models took the full channel test beside Claude. GLM 5.2 scored 76%, level with Sonnet 5. The scores are on /channel.
body: Native Yui runs on GLM through OpenRouter, so we put both GLM models through the same 88 turns the channel guide is tested on: timers, forms, plans, maps, music, photos, groups. A turn passes when the app can draw every line and the screen fits the ask. Claude Opus 5.5 passed 93%, Claude Sonnet 5 80%, GLM 5.2 76% and GLM-5V-Turbo 63%. Each model ran once, and every miss ran again, so a miss that holds up twice counts as real. GLM 5.2 misses mostly by running long. GLM-5V-Turbo is weaker at everyday turns, so Yui keeps it for photos only, where it passes. The defaults stay: GLM 5.2 for text, GLM-5V-Turbo for photos. Two things came out of it. GLM 5.2 sometimes spends its whole budget thinking and says nothing; that fix is on the board. And a new test turn, a lunch idea with the macros in a table, now guards against the broken table GLM wrote in a live run. A full GLM pass cost about 40 cents.

title: The first launch is Yui talking, with the crew already there
short: Open Yui for the first time and Yui is already talking, with your crew in the list. Nothing to pair, nothing to set up.
body: A new person used to land on an empty list and a pairing code. Now the app opens in Yui's thread with her first message on screen: who the crew is, and a choice of where to start. Arnold trains, Basil feeds you, Gouda makes music, Penny keeps your lists and Quill helps you study, and they are all in the list already, above any agent you pair from your own computer later. Remove one and Add agent offers it back: the crew sits at the top of that sheet by name, one tap each, next to pairing your own. A tap only ever adds; nothing already in your list changes, and one that is already there just opens its thread. Controls now shows each native agent's model by its name on the list Yui tests models against, and which profile it runs with its version. Tests: 4 new runtime tests (74 in all), database checks on a local copy of every migration (remove Basil, add him back, nothing else moves), and a first-launch UI test on a fresh simulator in light and dark. The screens here are the demo account playing the list the server makes; the live path is checked with the native release.

title: Your agents check in on their own
short: Tell Arnold "check in Monday at 7" and he does, with a push to your phone. Basil can ask about lunch every day at 12:30.
body: Native agents can set check-ins now. Say "check in Monday at 7" and the agent writes it down in your own time zone; the phone tells Yui which zone you are in. A clock on the server looks every minute for what is due, wakes the agent, and the agent opens the thread itself with a short line or a screen. Then your phone gets a push with its first words. Check-ins can be every day, weekdays, some days, once, or in two hours. You can pause one, run it now or delete it in the drawer's Controls tab. In a real run on GLM 5.2, Arnold heard "check in Monday at 7" and set it for Monday 7:00 in New York. When Monday came he opened with "Rise and grind! What's on tap today?" Basil set a lunch question for 12:30 every day and asked "Lunch time! What are you having today?" Both went through the real database code on a local copy, and the pushes landed on a simulator. Real iPhone pushes switch on once Yui's Apple push key is in place. It ships with the next TestFlight build.

If it finds no room it tries its short form ("Alvia via Ourense" without the hours), and if that fails too it is left off rather than drawn on top of something; VoiceOver still reads it. title: Your agents remember you, and you can fix what they remember
short: Tell one native agent something and every one of them knows it. Fix it in Controls and the very next answer uses the fix.
body: Native agents keep two kinds of memory. Each agent has its own notes (40 at most, oldest go first), and there is one About you card that every native agent on your Yui reads: your name, allergies, goals. Agents you pair from your own Mac never read it. The drawer's Controls tab shows both lists; edit a line or forget it there, with no chat turn, and the next answer reads the change. In a real run on GLM 5.2, Chris told Yui he is allergic to peanuts and training for a 10k. The card filled in by itself. We changed the allergy to peanuts and shellfish in Controls, then asked Basil for dinner ideas: his very next answer skipped both. Memory lives with your account, not your phone, so a new sign-in finds it all. The database now refuses a note on a paired agent or on someone else's agent, and a bug is fixed where two notes saved in one turn could swap numbers, so forget the first one could drop the wrong note. Tests: 8 new runtime tests (70 in all) and database checks on a local copy of every migration. Rides the native release.

The first run caught two bugs: the model wrote a stray end line that the phone showed as an error, and once it left its memory note unfenced, so you would have read it. Both are fixed. title: Native agents look things up, with sources
short: Native agents search the web and read pages and answer with their sources. 50 free lookups a month each; your own search key lifts the limit.
body: Ask a native agent something that needs today's facts and it looks it up, then answers with the pages it used as cards with a Read button. It can search, then read one page in full, two lookups a turn. Each person gets 50 free lookups a month on Yui's key (20 a day). When they run out, the agent answers from what it knows and shows one card, Free web searches used, whose button opens Settings at Web search. There you paste your own key from the search service: it is checked with the service, kept locked in the vault, shown only as its last four, and the limit goes away. It is never asked for in chat. 50 runtime tests, a migration checked on Postgres, and the tap from the card into Settings in light and dark. It goes live with the native sprint build.

title: Yui's own soul and first screen
short: Yui opens every new account with hello, your crew, and a question you answer with a tap.
body: Every native agent is now a folder of three files. profile.json holds its name, its role, its color, the Yui Lines it reaches for first and its model. soul.md says who it is, how it talks and what it never does. first.yui is its first answer: a line of text and a real question on a screen. Yui's own folder makes her a helper and a maker: she does the work herself, sends you to the right agent on your crew, and makes a new one when you ask. The build now loads every folder through the same checks the runtime uses and stops on any that fails: an unknown color, a screen the app cannot draw, a soul over 4000 characters, an em dash, or a first answer with no text before its screen. 52 of 52 runtime tests pass, 8 of them new for the loader and Yui's first turn. On a local run with a fresh account, Yui opened with her hello and the choice screen below, with no model called. It stays switched off until the native sprint build. title: Pick the model per turn
short: Native agents pick a model per turn: GLM 5.2 for words, GLM-5V-Turbo when you send a photo. First live run today, and it caught a bug.
body: The native runtime (YUI-130) now routes every turn through a small table: a turn with words goes to GLM 5.2, a turn with a photo or video goes to GLM-5V-Turbo, both on OpenRouter, with data collection turned off on every call. The base URL is plain OpenAI-compatible, so a person's own key for another provider slots in later. First live run: Basil answered a lunch question on GLM 5.2 in about 2 seconds, then read a real pizza photo on GLM-5V-Turbo and sent back macros per slice and a pick for how many you had. The same run caught a bug: Z.AI's image fetcher is turned away by some hosts, and the turn failed with an error in Chinese. Now the runtime fetches the photo itself and sends the bytes once more, so the answer still comes back. It also showed GLM 5.2 sometimes writes a table the wrong way; that goes to the channel eval next. The shots are Basil's answer drawn from Yui Lines on the site; native agents reach phones with the next release. `node runtime/scripts/live.ts` runs both turns with your own key.

short: A new map line draws countries, drawn borders, pins and routes, offline and in the agent's colors. On the web first, the app next.
body: Chris on the Mongol Empire answer in build 208: "Again, not bad but this should be a Map." The answer had a big number and four bullets, East, West, South and North. short: Ask any agent to help you tune up or keep time, and you get a tuner on the mic or a metronome, not a list of notes.

title: Yui 0.4.1 on the site: the release post
short: Build 208 is on TestFlight. A release post for musicians, and the roadmap says what is on phones.
body: Yui 0.4.1, build 208, is on TestFlight. The release post, Yui 0.4.1: tune up, keep time, send a take, walks through the four new music tools with shots and clips from the app: a tuner on the mic that turns green within 3 cents, a metronome in the chat that keeps time with a beat, Record on the looper, pads, keys and chords that sends the take to the agent, and a MIDI keyboard that plays the keys. It ends with a what to try checklist you can tap. The roadmap now says 0.4.1 is on phones, the music tools on See it say which build brought each one, and the changelog lists build 208's changes under build 208. They had been filed under build 204, because the export counted commits in a way a merged branch threw off.

title: See a take recorded and a keyboard played
short: See it plays two new clips from the app: a beat recorded and sent to the agent, and a MIDI keyboard playing the keys.
body: The music tools can now record, and See it shows it. Record a take: a boom bap loop plays, Record turns into Stop and send, and the agent gets the take as a sound file and a MIDI file, like a photo you took. Tap the sound on to hear the real take, 4.4 seconds, as the agent got it. A MIDI keyboard plays the keys: plug one in and each note lights up on screen and counts as played. Both clips are cut from real iPhone simulator captures. Still to come: a real keyboard on a real phone, the TestFlight build, and Ableton Link, which waits on a license call. The music spec says which is which, in section 8.

A MIDI keyboard holding C4 and E4: both keys lit on the screen

title: Record a take, plug in a keyboard
short: Record what you play on the looper, pads, keys or chords and the agent gets it as a sound file and a MIDI file. A MIDI keyboard plays the keys.
body: Step 5 of the music tools. Record sits on the looper, the drum pads, the keys and the chords. It records what Yui's sound engine plays, never the mic, to AAC at 48 kHz, up to 2 minutes. Stop and send uploads it the way a camera photo goes, and the agent gets two signed links: the .m4a and a .mid of the same take, with drums on channel 10 and each sound on its own track. Drum pads with +record now send their sound with the pattern. A MIDI keyboard over USB or Bluetooth plays the keys on screen: each note lights its key and counts as played, and the keys follow it to its octave. The MIDI button on the keys opens Apple's Bluetooth pairing screen. While the looper or the metronome plays, Yui sends MIDI clock, so a drum machine or a DAW follows its tempo. Proof, live on the simulator: a take recorded over a loop reached a real Yui host as two links, which opened with no key and held 4.4 s of AAC, 48000 Hz, 2 channels and a MIDI file with 27 drum hits, and the agent answered with the take as a link (14 of 14 checks). In the UI tests a virtual keyboard lit and played the keys, and the clock arrived 24 a beat, 20.83 ms apart at 120 BPM. Ableton Link waits on a sign-off of its license: the SDK may not be given to anyone, and Yui's code is public. A real keyboard on a phone comes with the next TestFlight build.

title: A clean sweep after Yui 0.4.0
short: Every page, link, clip, share card and library screen on the site checked after the 0.4.0 night. One fix: the tuner's share card.
body: After a night of Yui 0.4.0 pages, clips and Thoughts, the site got its full check. The link check walked 346 pages, 1,421 internal links and images and 1,240 anchors: all good. The library check drew 44 presets, 5 flows and 5 music screens: all good. The freshness check read 105 files against build 204: all good. The share card check found one gap. The new tuner and metronome entry had no capture of its screen, so its share link drew a simpler picture. It now shows the real tuner, ukulele strings and all, at /s/tuner-in-app.

title: Agents send keys and chords
short: Ask any agent for something to play in a key, or a song's chords, and you get a keyboard or chord buttons, not a list of notes.
body: Build 204 draws the keyboard and the chord buttons, so channel guide v33 teaches every agent the two lines. `keys Am pentatonic` is a keyboard in a key: notes outside the scale are locked, so nothing sounds wrong. `chords G I-V-vi-IV` (or by name, `chords C|G|Am|F`) is a song's chords as big buttons to strum, and `~chords key=D` moves them. `+send` on either sends back what you played. Two new eval cases: A minor pentatonic on piano, and a four chord song on a uke in G. The v32 guide scored 0 of 2 (a drum loop with the note names in words, and a drum loop with a card of uke chord shapes); v33 sent `keys Am pentatonic` and `chords G I-V-vi-IV +send`, 2 of 2. The older music, plain and short cases held, and on the full suite v33 scored inside the old guide's range, so the held "Show, don't say" rule ships with it. The music screens in the library now show as ready for the app, except the ones with a tuner or a metronome, which join with the next TestFlight build. Phones older than build 177 get the keyboard and the chords in words.

title: A tuner and a metronome in the app
short: Tune a guitar, ukulele or bass on the mic, and practice to a click that keeps time with your beat.
body: Step 4 of the music tools. tuner listens through the mic, lights the nearest string and shows how far off it is on a needle from -50 to +50 cents. Within 3 cents the needle turns green. Every string is a button that plays its note, so you can tune by ear, and that still works if you say no to the mic. When every string has held in tune for a second, the agent gets one message with each string's cents. Guitar standard, drop D and DADGAD, ukulele with a high or low G, 4 and 5 string bass, custom strings, a4=442 and a chromatic mode are in. The mic is on only while the tuner listens; nothing is recorded or sent. metronome sits in the chat: a big tempo, Tap tempo, a dot per beat with the first one accented, and clicks on the beat, in eighths, triplets or sixteenths. It runs on the same clock as the looper, so a click under a beat lands on its beat, and it keeps going with the phone locked. Stop after 10 seconds tells the agent how long you practiced. Tests: tones at known offsets on every string of every tuning read within 2 cents (sine tones within 0.01), and the metronome held every click within 0.1 ms of a click track for 5 minutes at four tempos. Tuning a real guitar and ukulele on a phone comes next; it rides the next TestFlight build.

title: The picture listens
short: In the app, the live picture behind the words moves with your voice, the agent's voice and the music. Yui 0.4.0, build 204.

body: Chris asked for About and Controls to be one tab in the drawer, since both are about the agent. It is written down with the files it touches and the tests to update, and it waits in the app backlog. Nothing changed on the phone yet, so there is no picture.

title: Hermes for everyone: the spec
body: How a person with no server gets a hosted Hermes agent inside Yui, with their own key and their own data. This is a written spec, so there is nothing to screenshot. It is live on the site.

title: Native Yui: the spec
body: Yui's plan for a native Yui: every person gets their own Yui and a starter crew at sign-in, with the engine on the phone. This is a written spec, so there is nothing to screenshot. It is live on the site.

title: Every drum name plays a real drum
short: Name a loop row surdo, caixa or ganza and it plays that kind of drum, not a tick.
body: A beat with rows named the way a musician would say them, like a samba with surdo, caixa, tamborim and ganza, used to tick on every row. Now each name plays a matching drum, and a name the kit does not know takes the next unused voice, so no two rows share one. Open the samba in the playground and press play.

short: What waits on you lives in the drawer now: Home for the status, Review for the asks.
body: Chris: the war room should not be a screen you swipe to, it should live in the drawer. Now it does. Home shows the status, the busy lanes and the queue. Review lists what waits on you, and a tap on a row opens its question as one choice with no agent turn in between. The old screen 2 path is gone.

body: Test builds used to install over the real app and replace it. They now ship as Yui Dev, with a DEV badge on the icon and their own app id, so both live on the phone side by side. Push, sign-in and links know about the second app. Push on the Dev copy was not tested on its own.

body: Chris, from TestFlight: "Users can get to the chat view on the top right. We'll have to find room on the top left hamburger tab for the settings themselves, maybe to the left of the selector for the agents." Now the top of the full screen is three things. title: A live picture behind the words
short: Agents can now put a moving picture behind the stage, in their own colors, that moves with a voice or music. Try it in the playground.

title: Say how each agent moves
short: Describe how an agent should move, in your own words, and it saves a motion look next to its colors.
body: Chris wanted people to just describe the animation each agent gets. Now you can. Say "make it heavy and punchy" and the agent writes one Yui Lines line, theme pace=quick ease=heavy enter=drop pulse=beat, and saves it with its colors. Four words make a look: pace (slow, even, quick), ease (float, spring, sharp, heavy), how things come on (rise, pop, slide, drop, fade) and how it breathes (soft, beat, tick, still). The mock at /playground?demo=motion-looks plays one turn on two agents: Coach was told heavy and punchy, Sage drifts like water. Type your own words and the stage moves that way at once. A small word table does it on the web, the agent uses its own judgment. Every parser reads the new keys, and Reduce Motion still holds everything still. The app reads the saved look next, with the stage motion build.

body: Chris, Sep 26: "These images could be bigger... I wanna make sure we're not cutting off screenshots or really any type of image. When displaying an image, we should look at the size of the actual image and then create a box that big instead." Now every picture waits for its real size and draws in a box that shape: a photo, a gallery, a storyboard, a picture in the chat. The stage opens from the mic, parts come on in the agent's own way and the questions arrive one by one. The look has room for YUI-123, where you describe how an agent moves in words. title: Send answers in about 70 ms
short: Tap Send and your bubble is up in about 70 ms, under the 100 ms target.
body: The last 30 ms from YUI-106. Send used to take about 127 ms to answer; now it is 64 to 95 ms on the simulator with a 500 message thread, against 162 for the old code in the same session. The big one: after a send, Yui swaps in a fresh text field so the sent words are sure to clear, and that swap reloads the keyboard. It ran before the frame with your bubble reached the screen. Now it waits two frames. Smaller ones: the field empties before the bubble goes in, the bubble and the working row move in one step, and the working row is drawn once, unseen, before your first send. Nothing looks different. The keyboard still dips for a moment after Send, from the same field swap; that goes only if a way to clear the field without a new one holds up on a real phone. Real phone numbers come from the next TestFlight build.

title: The full screen stage, drawn
short: A playground mock of Yui living on the full screen: the answer plays in parts, the questions come last, the chat is the record.
body: Your first message opens the whole screen right away, no typing dots. While the agent works you see your words, a soft shape breathing and what it is doing. Then the answer plays in short parts, a line and a drawing each; a status question is one screen. The questions wait for the end, all on one screen with one Send, and everything lands in the chat, top right, where a tap reopens any part. The new bars are in it too: settings and your agent top left, a bigger mic bottom right (tap and talk, your words stream in), taken a notch smaller after Chris's first look, T to open the text field and + to attach, with photos sitting in the field while you type. Settings turn T and + on or off. Nothing changes on the wire: YL.md now says how any reply plays this way, and the guide gets a Show, don't say rule, drafted and scored but not sent to agents yet. Open it at yuigui.com/playground?demo=stage-first. The app follows once Chris picks.

title: Help: why a beat is silent
short: Help now answers "I asked for a beat and hear nothing": the silent switch, and how to play.
body: On Yui 0.3.2 the ring/silent switch mutes the looper and the drum pads. That was Chris's first try at a beat. The fix is on main and rides the next build. Until then, /help says to flip the switch and turn the volume up, and gives one line each on asking for a beat, tapping cells, the drum pads and Record, with a link to the music demo in the playground. A text-only change, so no screenshots.

title: Agents send a beat
short: Ask any agent for a beat and you get one you can play and edit. Drum pads too.
body: Build 176 draws the looper and the drum pads, so channel guide v31 teaches every agent the two lines. A beat is one line: `loop 96 "Boom bap" p=x...x.x.|....x...|xxxxxxxx +play`, one string per row, x a hit, a dot a rest. Pads are `drums 2x2`, and `+record` sends a take back as a beat. When you tap Send, your version comes back to the agent in the same words, so it patches it in and saves it to your shelf. On three new eval cases the old guide scored 0 of 3 (a drum table in markdown, a tic-tac-toe game for the pads, a re-sent loop); v31 scored 3 of 3. Keys, chords, the tuner and the metronome join the guide as their builds land. Phones older than build 175 get the beat in words.

Dark mode: the same Boom bap looper playing, eight rows from kick to shaker, the hat row lit on every step.

The release post, Yui 0.3.2: ask any agent for a beat, leads with the looper and drum pads that now play in the app, then hold to reply, the quiet dot on the menu button, the working row that says what the agent is doing and how long it usually takes, and a what to try checklist you can tick. See it has a Yui 0.3.2 group with six entries from real simulator captures, and the music group's loop and drums now read as in the app. The roadmap says 0.3.2 is on phones and marks YUI-116 step 2, YUI-63 step 2 and YUI-107 shipped. The changelog and the board are synced to build 176.

title: It says what it is doing
short: The working row shows what your agent is doing, with a bar when it knows the steps.
body: Chris's words: "the agent sends a few words on what it is doing, with a small progress bar when it knows the steps." From build 176 (Yui 0.3.2) the working row under your message reads Reading your calendar, then Checking the weather, then Drafting the plan, with a thin bar in the agent's color and the seconds still counting. The reply clears it. It is never a bubble and never sends a push. The host writes the newest words onto your message while the turn runs, about once a second, and only to phones that draw them; older builds keep Pondering. Channel guide v30 tells every agent to do it in plain words, no ids or file names: the old guide sent none on a long turn, v30 sent three, two runs of two.

title: Short answers first
short: A status question gets one line now, and a deck is four pages at most.
body: Chris, Sep 26: "this last full screen header had eight screens of basically nothing just to tell me that I'm up-to-date." The channel guide sent anything over about 50 words to a deck, so agents padded a yes into four pages and a go-ahead into eight. Guide v29 turns that around. The first line is the answer. A yes/no or status question gets one line or one card, never a deck. A deck needs three or more things to read, holds four pages at most, and drops any page that repeats the headline or says what happens next with nothing to act on. Two new eval cases replay the screenshot: the old guide failed both (49 words to say yes, a timeline for a go-ahead), the new one answers "Yes, this phone is on build 160, the newest. Your iPad is still on 135." A new page cap keeps the report cases at four pages; the old replies had five and six. Every agent on the Yui channel gets it on its next turn.

images.alt: Light mode: a before and after sketch for Am I on the latest build. Before, a long reply struck out, noted 4 pages to say yes. After, one highlighted line: Yes, build 160, the newest. Your iPad is on 135.
Dark mode: the same before and after sketch, the long reply struck out and the one-line answer highlighted.

title: Keys and chords you can play in the app
short: An easy keyboard with a scale lock and big chord buttons that strum, played through Yui's own sound engine.
body: Step 3 of the music tools. keys puts one octave and a bit on the phone. The scale lock is on by default, so keys outside the key are dimmed and make no sound, and nothing you play sounds wrong. Arrows move an octave up or down, a picker switches between six sounds (keys, pluck, bell, pad, bass, lead), every finger plays its own note, and sliding across the keys plays each one. Send hands the agent the notes you played. chords turns a key and a progression like I-V-vi-IV into one big button per chord, with the name large and the numeral under it, or takes chord names like C|G|Am|F. A tap strums it down, up or all at once, on the same clock as the looper and the pads. When an agent writes ~chords key=D, every chord moves to D and keeps its numeral. A test checks every numeral form in the spec in all 12 major and 12 minor keys. It rides the next TestFlight build.

Dark mode: four chord buttons in G labeled G I, D V, Em vi and C IV, strum buttons Down, Up and Off, and the chords played so far.

title: Music screens agents can find
short: Five ready-made music screens in the library: a practice session, a chord chart, a beat to jam over, a songwriting check-in and a scale warm-up.
body: The six music presets were in the spec, but an agent looking for music found nothing. Now the library has five ready-made music screens, each a whole reply built from the presets: a practice session (tune up, a click, then a loop to play over), a chord chart for a song, a beat to jam over, a songwriting check-in and a scale warm-up. They sit on the music shelf of the library, drawn live and ready to open in the playground, and /api/library?q=music and the yui_library MCP tool return them, marked as coming to the app. The music page links each one. The line that teaches agents to reach for music is written and waiting in the channel guide: it goes live with the app build that draws the looper and drum pads, so no phone gets a screen it cannot play yet.

title: The working row says how long it usually takes
short: While an agent works, the row under it says how long its turns usually take, like an iPhone install.
body: Chris, Sep 26: "Would be good if there was some expectation on how long it will take in the counter... similar to like when you install new software on an iPhone." The counter only counted up. Now the phone keeps how long each agent's recent turns took, from pickup to finished, and once it has three it says the usual range under the row: Usually 1 to 3 min. One odd long turn does not stretch it. Past the top of the range it says Longer than usual, and after two minutes that you can leave and the answer lands here. VoiceOver reads it too.

title: Yui for musicians: the plan, and a mock that plays
body: Chris wants Yui to be a musician's best friend, so music is now the app's main focus. Step 1 is the plan and a working mock. Six new instruments, one line each: a step looper (loop), drum pads (drums), an easy keyboard with a scale lock so nothing sounds wrong (keys), big chord buttons from a key and a progression like I-V-vi-IV (chords), a tuner for guitar, ukulele, bass or any note (tuner), and a metronome. An agent can write a beat, you edit it, and Send hands the pattern back so it can be saved. The agent can change a playing instrument live, like ~chords key=D. All six share one sound engine with 21 voices, rebuilt from the synth recipes behind the brag film, and agents name sounds by word (sound=pluck), never by file. The spec covers the research: the apps people love, iOS audio and latency, how the tuner hears pitch, MIDI and Ableton Link. Every hub parser reads the new lines. The playground plays all of it in your browser today, tuner included. The app gets the engine, the looper and the drum pads next.
short: Six music tools, one line each, on one sound engine. The mock plays in your browser.

title: Agents make their own flows: variants
body: An agent can now make its own version of a saved flow without copying it. It names the flow it starts from, gives the new one a name, and says only what changes: drop a step, reword one, add one after another. Scout turns the client website intake into a restaurant intake in six lines: ask what kind of place, drop the pages and product questions, add the menu and online orders. The phone keeps a variant as its base plus those lines, so fixing the base fixes every variant made from it, and flow restaurant-intake runs it again later. The JavaScript, Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers read variants and pass the same 23 new vectors, 683 each. The library lists the restaurant intake under the website intake with its chart, the changed steps dashed, and /api/library finds it. Try it: /playground?demo=flow-variant. Spec: /developers/flows#9-variants. The app runs flows next.
short: Agents make their own version of a saved flow in a few lines. Try the restaurant intake in the playground.

title: Yui is in alpha: a Thought on how the MVP got done
body: A new Thought, Yui is in alpha, tells the story behind today's MVP call. It walks the six steps the MVP promised, each with a real capture: install from the public TestFlight link, Sign in with Apple, pair your own agent with a six-digit code, screens back that you can change your mind on (a live choose screen you can tap), a push when your agent answers, and deleting your account from Settings, with a fresh shot of the delete sheet. Then four days from the first TestFlight build on Sep 23 to alpha on Sep 26, drawn live as two stats (34 builds) and a timeline. It says plainly what alpha means for a stranger: Yui is the screen and you bring the agent (Hermes, OpenClaw, MCP, A2A, a webhook or a local model); there is no hosted agent yet. It ends with the queue: the stranger acceptance run first, then flows in the app, group threads and a working row that says what your agent is doing, plus one line to use to earn. It is in the RSS feed and has its own share preview.

images.alt: The Yui is in alpha Thought on a phone: the Four days section, a live Yui screen with 4 days from first build to alpha, Sep 23 to Sep 26, 34 TestFlight builds, and a How it got here timeline starting First build on TestFlight.

title: Flows and the library: a Thought on screens any agent can run

title: The MVP is done: Yui is in alpha, and use to earn begins
body: Chris called the MVP done on Sep 26, and Yui is in alpha: open to anyone with an iPhone on iOS 26 through TestFlight. The site says so everywhere, and every call to action reads Download on TestFlight. The home page is rebuilt around it: a big horizontal video at the top (a stand-in until the new hero video is ready), two buttons, Download on TestFlight and Star on GitHub, and eight of the best screen recordings from around the site, each playing as you scroll past. A short new section teases use to earn: the people who use Yui early, and help build it, should earn a stake in it. The thinking is in a new business doc, Use to earn. The record behind it is a private ledger, designed and tested: facts about use and contributions back to day one, never what anyone said. It starts recording when Chris switches it on. No token exists and nothing is for sale.

title: Outside agents draw like the app
body: The Yui MCP server checks every screen an outside agent sends with its own copy of the Yui Lines parser, and that copy had fallen behind the app and the site. A doing line, the working row that says what the agent is up to, came back as an unknown preset. The copy is current again and deployed, and the live test sends a doing line through yui_show and gets it back accepted (114 of 114 checks). So it can't slip again, the app repo's checks now compare the copy with the site's parser on every push and once a day, and fail when they differ.

title: Agents can look up the library
body: The library at yuigui.com/developers/library now answers agents too. Ask /api/library?q=client intake and the client website intake flow comes back first, with the line that runs it and its Mermaid. Every entry has a few plain intent phrases ("get a client's website brief", "ask a yes or no question"), and one search ranks them the same way on the page, at the endpoint and in the new yui_library tool on the Yui MCP server. It is plain word matching, no model behind it. The channel guide, v28, names the five saved flows and says to send one instead of building a plan when it fits. Tested on a client who wants a bakery site: the old guide built ten questions by hand, the new one sent flow website-intake. The library gained the shapes diagram tiles it was missing, and a check now runs before every site build, so a screen can no longer ship without its tile. Also fixed: the Rust parser now lowercases a shape's kind like the others, and a new check holds all four hub parsers to it.
short: Agents can search the library by intent, on the site or over MCP, and the guide points them at the saved flows.

title: Speed numbers are stored once
body: The first speed numbers from a real phone showed one batch stored twice, 19 seconds apart, across a relaunch. The phone keeps a batch until the server answers, so a send that lands just as iOS puts the app away goes again on the next launch. Now every row gets its own random key when it is made, kept with it on the phone, and the server skips a key it already has: the resend still answers OK and nothing is stored twice. Proof: the live table tests (91 of 91, 11 new), the app's own tests (12 of 12) and a simulator run where the app sent 3 stored rows again plus 1 new one, and only the new one landed. No screen changes, so no screenshots. It rides the next TestFlight release.

title: Every share link shows its real screen

That phone is a capture of the real screen. 58 of the 219 share links had none on the live site, so their previews drew a plain stand-in instead: the flow screen showed one button where the app shows a whole step. All 58 are captured and live now, and three older ones that had drifted (the timeline, restyle and the release timeline) were taken again. One sample named a private agent in its header; it reads Scout now. A new check, npm run og, fails when a share link has no capture or names a private agent, and it runs on every push.

title: Help catches up with the app
body: The Help page (/help, the app's support link) was checked against the app on main, answer by answer. Two answers named steps that moved: a pairing code that ran out now says tap Get a new code, and the notifications switch now lives in the agent's menu, under Controls, then Name, look and notifications. title: Sync, decided: not in v1
body: Agent tables live on your iPhone. The question was whether Yui v1 should copy them to a second device. The answer is no: v1 is one iPhone, and the real risk, a new phone with an empty workout log, is covered by keeping the tables in the phone's own backup. The design is written anyway, for the day a Mac, iPad or browser version of Yui arrives. Sync is off by default and needs no new account. Only agent tables sync, never chats or keys. Every change is sealed on the phone, and Yui's server holds boxes it cannot open: no table names, no columns, no values. A second device joins by scanning a QR code from Settings, and you confirm it with Face ID. Two devices editing the same row agree without asking you, and the same agent reply seen on two devices makes one row, not two. Removing a device makes a new key, and turning sync off deletes the server's copy at once while every device keeps its own tables. No new Yui Lines word. Try it in the playground; five questions for Chris end the spec.
short: Tables stay on your iPhone in v1. Encrypted sync is designed for when a second device arrives.

title: The war room, stripped down
body: Chris, Sep 26: "the war room is an absolute mess. I respond to cards and they don't go away, it's long as can be and there's a big library at the bottom." Screen 2 now holds four things: one folded status line (the build on your phone, what waits on main, where the release stands), at most three asks with their context above the buttons, one Now and next timeline with a row per busy lane and the queue you can drag, and one link to the board. The release checklist, commit list, builds, speed tiles, feedback cards, MVP stat and eight link cards are gone; the page went from 56 lines to 15, about a third of its old height. Rows read as plain words, never a card id plus a raw comment. Answering an ask now redraws the war room right after the tap, so the card leaves at once. 22 war room tests and 22 plugin tests pass.

title: Designed in the open: a Thought on how Yui designs in public
body: A new Thought, Designed in the open, tells how a Yui feature starts: a spec page and a mock you can tap in the playground, before any app code. It walks the five designs that went up today (the starter agent, widgets and Siri, the model on the phone, the key vault, a lesson as one deck), each with its playground mock and links, and the rules they share: keys never in chat, the phone's model never speaks as an agent, the agent never sees a key. It ends with an invitation for agents to pick one up.

title: A lesson is one deck
body: Follow-up to Chris's Sep 26 feedback: "I want all that to be in one experience." A deck page can now hold a diagram, a formula, a chart, a big number or a calculator as its picture, the same way it already held a sketch. So a lesson is one swipeable deck: an idea per page, each with its picture, a quiz, and the sliders on the last page. The change is in all five parsers (JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin, Rust) with new conformance vectors, the site's playground and the app. A slider drag moves the slider, not the page. Phones on older builds still get the pieces laid out on one full screen, so nothing breaks before the update lands. The channel guide now asks for one deck.
short: A lesson is one swipeable deck: diagram, formula, chart, number, quiz, then the sliders.

title: Every link on the site resolves
body: A built-in-public site with dead links reads as stale, so now a script checks. It crawls all 273 pages in the sitemap and tries every link, image, clip, poster and #anchor on them, about 1,300 in all. Anything broken fails the run with the file and line it came from: a progress entry, See it, the roadmap or a spec. The first run found 7 dead links, all between spec pages: a link written as FLOWS.md works on GitHub but pointed nowhere on the site. Spec pages now send those links to the right page, and the check passes. Links to other sites are tried too and reported, but never fail the run, since other sites go down. This card is a script, so there is nothing new to see.

title: A key vault, planned
body: Some things agents do cost money at another company: an image from fal, a model through OpenRouter, Anthropic or OpenAI, a run on Replicate. Today paying for that with your own account means a key in a file on the machine the agent runs on. The plan puts your keys on your iPhone instead. A key goes in one way only, Settings > Keys: paste it or scan it off your computer screen, never into a chat or an agent's form. It stays in the Keychain on this phone, and after you save it you only ever see its last four characters. When an agent needs one it asks through its host, and Yui draws the ask itself, so no agent can fake it: Penny wants to use your fal key to draw your agent avatars, with Allow, Allow once and Don't allow. Yui's hosted connector gets the key sealed and makes the call; the agent gets a handle and never sees the key. Every key has a monthly cap, every call lands in an activity list, and the drawer shows what each agent may use, with Revoke. No new word in Yui Lines. Try it in the playground with placeholder keys. Seven questions for Chris end the spec; building it natively is the next step.
short: Keys live in your iPhone's Keychain. Agents ask, you allow, they never see the key.

The channel guide says it in one rule, and a new eval case checks every piece lands on the full screen. The old guide scattered them (0 of 1), the new one passes (1 of 1) with no slip on plain answers, diagrams or reports. It is live for every agent now, with no app update. Next, a deck page will hold these pieces, so a lesson can be one swipeable deck.

title: Faster pages, and every one clears 90
body: A speed and accessibility pass on the seven busiest pages, measured with Lighthouse on a phone profile. Before: the home page scored 80 for speed, See it 67 and the roadmap 71; the rest were 94 to 100. After, taking the middle of three runs: home 100, See it 99, roadmap 99, Shipped 98, Developers 100, Get Yui 100, playground 96. Accessibility went from 95 to 98 on four pages to 100 on all seven, and Best Practices stays at 100. What changed: the analytics tag waits until the page has loaded, the live phones fetch their drawing code only when one scrolls near, the videos on See it load their cover frames as you reach them, the logo is a 6KB image instead of 27KB, and the row of section links under the menu no longer downloads every page in the section up front. For accessibility: headings now step down in order, the big coral numbers on the home page use the darker coral that reads on cream, and screenshot thumbnails keep their size before they load, so they are easy to tap. Nothing you see moved.

title: What you were typing stays put
body: Chris, Sep 26: "I was writing in the text box and then a new answer came in and took over the screen with a full screen. But then when I came back my query was lost." Each agent's thread now keeps its own unsent words on the phone, saved as you type and cleared when you send. A reply going full screen, switching to another agent, leaving the app or closing it all leave the words where they were. A new test types, lets the agent open a full screen, closes it and checks the words are still there, then checks each agent keeps its own draft across a relaunch. The composer, keyboard, full screen and typing speed tests still pass. It rides the next release.
short: Half-typed words stay in the box through a full screen, another agent or a relaunch.

title: The model on the phone, planned
body: Newer iPhones carry a language model of their own, and apps can use it for free, with nothing leaving the phone. The plan gives it four small jobs in Yui. When an agent asks something in words, two or three reply chips show under the screen; a tap sends one as your message. In a group, a pill over the composer says who your message is for (To Sage, sleep and calm), and Change picks someone else. A reply that is all screen gets a real line on the lock screen instead of "Coach has something for you in Yui". With no signal, a typed ask gets a draft checklist or timer, marked as a draft, while the message waits for the agent. It never answers as an agent and never sends without a tap. Phones without Apple Intelligence keep the app as it is today. Try all four in the playground, with a switch to turn the model off. Seven questions for Chris end the spec; building it natively is the next step.
short: Reply chips, the right agent in a group, better push lines and offline drafts, all on your phone.

title: Widgets and Siri, planned
body: Today an agent's screen lives in its thread: to check your weight trend or tick off today's list you open Yui and find it. The plan takes Yui out of the app. A widget is a saved screen you pin to the home screen or the lock screen: a stat with its trend, a checklist, a timer. The agent keeps it current with the same patches it already sends, and Yui's relay tells the widget to redraw with a WidgetKit push, so it never polls and stays inside Apple's budget of 40 to 70 refreshes a day. Tick a row or start the timer right on the widget and the agent gets the same event as a tap in the thread. Siri gets three things to do: ask an agent, show a saved screen, start a timer, and one of them can live on the Action button. No new word in Yui Lines. Try the home screen, the lock screen and Siri in the playground. Seven questions for Chris end the spec; building it natively is the next step.
short: Pin a saved screen to your home or lock screen, tap it without opening Yui, and ask Siri.

title: A starter agent, planned and priced
body: Today someone who downloads Yui with no agent of their own gets an empty list. The plan to fix it is written: pick Coach, Basil, Penny or Quill on first launch and it answers right away, no computer needed. It runs on Yui's hosted connector beside the relay, on the person's own OpenRouter account first (one sign-in, no key to paste), with no tools that act on the world, caps per turn, per person and for the whole host, and a kill switch. The cost model prices a turn at about a tenth of a cent on a cheap model and one cent on a frontier one, and a month at 100 to 10,000 people. It ends with five questions for Chris: who pays, which model, how big a free tier. Try the first launch in the playground. Building it needs a Cloudflare account and spend, so that waits on Chris.

title: Talk to your agents hands-free, read the answers
body: Chris, Sep 24: "human voice in, text out, fast and smooth." Tap the mic once and Yui keeps listening between turns. Your words show as you say them, a short pause sends them, the answer comes back as text, and the mic opens again once it lands. The bar says where you are: Listening, Sending, on it, Your turn, or Paused. One button stops it. A call or an alarm pauses it and it picks up after; leaving the app stops it. Holding the mic still works the old way. Speech now runs on Apple's new on-device transcriber, and the audio never leaves your phone, only the text. Measured on the same spoken clip: the final words land about 90 ms after you stop talking (under 600 ms the first time). While an answer is owed, Yui checks for it every 350 ms instead of every 1.5 s, so it shows up sooner. Each agent can start with typing or talking, in its settings. It rides the next release.
short: Tap the mic, talk, pause: it sends, the answer comes back as text, and the mic opens again.

title: A full screen takes the keyboard down with it
body: Chris, Sep 26: "if I ever open a full screen, I need the keyboard to go away automatically." He was typing, opened a diagram full screen, and the keyboard stayed up over the bottom third of it. Now any full screen drops the keyboard as it opens: a reply the agent opens on its own, a pill in the chat, a deck, a plan, a picture, the camera. Closing it leaves the keyboard down, and what you typed is still in the field. A new test types in the chat, opens a full screen and checks the keyboard is gone. It rides the next release.
short: Opening anything full screen puts the keyboard away, and closing it keeps it down.

title: Yui holds less in memory, and a test checks it before every release
body: Chris, Sep 25: "I think there must be memory leakage all over the place." We measured first. A scripted session on the simulator opens five agents with 486-message threads, galleries, decks, games and screens 2 to 12, goes full screen, then idles, while the app logs its memory every second and a leak checker runs at the start and the end. The big leak was the deck you swipe inside a message: every one that scrolled out of the thread left its pages behind, about 1,550 leaked objects over one session. It pages with a plain scroll now, and the session ends with zero new leaks. Pictures used to decode at full size for as long as their message lived; now each is decoded at the size it is drawn and shares one cache with a size limit that empties when the phone runs low. Videos let go of their player when they leave the screen, a long thread drops the older rows it drew once you are back at the bottom, and a few lists that only ever grew are gone or trimmed. The session's peak fell from 243 MB to 203 MB and launch from 137 MB to 124 MB, with taps and scrolling as fast as before. The same session now runs before every release and fails on new leaks, growth or a peak over 300 MB. It rides the next release.
short: Yui uses less memory: peak down from 243 to 203 MB in a long session, and no new leaks.

title: A timeline opened on its own sits at the top
body: A saved screen holding only a timeline, opened full screen from the shelf, used to spread three rows over the whole phone: big empty gaps, and the running row's highlight about 400 points tall. The rows' dot column was flexible, so they soaked up the extra height the full screen hands its content. Now each row keeps its natural height and a timeline starts at the top, like a page you read down. A card, timer or stat alone still sits in the middle. The folded 'earlier' button's line was fixed the same way. It rides the next release.
short: A timeline opened full screen keeps its rows tight and starts at the top.

After: the same timeline full screen, the done row, Now line, running row and queued row packed together at the top

title: Agent tables in the Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers
body: The web half of step 2 for agent tables. The Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers now read table create, put and query, and each carries its own copy of the store: upsert by key, rows that append with no key, today and now dates, where filters, sort with empty cells last, group and totals. The table vectors moved out of the JavaScript-only file, so every runner in the repo checks all 36 of them against its own store: 591 of 591 pass in Python, Kotlin and Rust, and JavaScript still passes all 612. The app half, the same store in SQLite on the phone, comes next. A spec and parser change, nothing new to see.

title: Every agent can put a picture on a page
body: The channel guide every agent reads on Yui (v23) now teaches the page picture: in a walkthrough deck or plan, a small drawing right after a page is that page's picture, the before struck out and the after highlighted. Phones have drawn it since build 104; 0.3.0 (build 138) has it. One example line costs about 93 tokens a turn. Scored on a new eval case, walk me through three changes with a before and after for each: the v22 guide sent loose drawings with no pages, v23 put one on each page. A first draft let one run put a moving diagram inside the deck, which ends it; one clause fixed that, and the report, drawing and plain-answer cases all still pass. Published to every agent on Yui and sent for real: Yui walked Chris through it as two pages, the first with its drawing.
short: Walkthrough pages can carry their own before and after drawing, and every agent on Yui now knows how.

images.alt: A Yui deck titled Pages with pictures: page 1 shows a drawn chat bubble, 'Parked YUI-83 in the backlog' struck out and 'Parked the drawing card in the backlog' highlighted, above the page title The page shows it

title: Talk about a setting, built: change your agent by talking
body: Step 2 of 2. Every item in Controls (the personality, a memory, a skill, a schedule, and the model card, read only) now has a Talk about this button. It closes the drawer and pins the item above the composer as a chip: tap it to see the item, x to take it off, and a second item replaces the first. Say what you want and your message goes out with a short line naming the item, never its text. Your Mac puts the item into the agent's turn itself, with any line holding a key hidden. The agent proposes, it never writes: your Mac checks the change with the same rules as a hand edit and draws it in the chat as a before and after, with Apply and Keep it as is. Apply writes it with no agent turn, keeps the old copy and logs it, and a card says it is done. If the file changed on your Mac meanwhile, nothing is written and Ask again gets a fresh proposal. A memory with a key in it can be talked about but never changed from the phone. Only the owner can do any of this. Tested end to end on the simulator over the live relay: a new line in SOUL.md, one Keep it as is, a terminal edit mid-proposal, a memory forgotten, a schedule moved to 7:30, and nothing key-shaped in the messages. Rides the next release.
short: Tap Talk about this on any setting, say what you want, and Apply the before and after your agent proposes.

title: Send and the menu drawer answer faster
body: A follow-up to the smooth release. Opening the menu drawer now answers in about 66 ms, down from 104 to 172, and the jitter between runs is gone. Send got faster too, from about 170 ms to 127, but not yet under the 100 ms target, so YUI-108 takes the last 30. The fixes: saving a sent message happens off the main thread, the drawer is built out of sight right after the thread opens, and the list of what is waiting on you is worked out once per change instead of on every draw. Measured on the simulator with a 500-message thread, three paired runs. Rides the next release.

title: The app moves timeline rows in place
body: Step 2 of 2. The iPhone app now reads `kind=` on a timeline row patch: `~rel-YUI-202 kind=done` turns a running card done where it stands and the Now line moves past it, on the page and in its saved copy on the shelf. The Swift, Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers all learned it, so the 12 test vectors run in every language now (545 each, 602 in JavaScript). The war room uses it next: once the phone is on build 143 or newer, a card moving on the board reaches the release panel as one quiet patch line instead of the whole page and a push. It rides the next release.

title: Yui@home runs every week: a routine for each agent
body: Step 2. /contribute now has a weekly routine for Claude, ChatGPT Codex, Google Jules, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and any agent that can run the GitHub CLI. Paste one in, and your agent takes one open card a week, stays inside a budget you pick, and stops when nothing is open. We checked every setup against that platform's own docs today, and the links sit under each prompt. Our finding: none of them documents forking a repo you don't own. So the hosted routines work in your fork and hand back a one-click link for the pull request, and the Actions recipe does the whole thing with your own token. Every pull request now runs the same checks in both repos (conformance vectors, bench tests, the site build, the Swift parser) with no secrets. CI, signing and release files need the owner's review, and nothing merges on its own. When a pull request titled with a card key merges, the card closes and leaves the backlog by itself. Your GitHub handle goes on this page only if you tick Credit me.

title: A timeline row can move without resending the page
body: Step 1 of 2. A patch can now change a timeline row's kind: `~rel-YUI-54 kind=done` turns a running card done in place, and the Now line moves past it. Before, a card changing status meant sending the whole page again, which jumped the screen and pushed a notification. Now it is one quiet line. The row keeps its place and its id. Written into the Yui Lines spec and the release panel spec, with 12 new test vectors, and live in the playground: pick the timeline sample and press Send on the agent line. The app learns it in step 2, then the war room's release panel switches to it.

title: Agent controls, built: your agent's settings in the drawer
body: Step 2 of 2. The drawer's Controls tab now talks to the Mac the agent runs on. Read and edit its personality file, forget one memory, switch a skill off and on, pause a schedule, resume it or run it now, and see its model and channels. A change lands on the Mac in about a second, with no chat turn, and the agent hears about it in one line on its next turn. Every delete asks first. If the Mac changed the same thing since you opened it, you see both versions and pick one. A line with a key in it never leaves the Mac: it shows as hidden and that item stays read only. Only the owner sees Controls; someone an agent is shared with never does, and the relay refuses it too. Rides the next release.

title: Yui@home: the agent-ready backlog is live
body: Lend your agent to Yui now works end to end on our side. Cards marked agent-ready on our board are exported to /contribute and to /contribute/backlog.json, each with its goal, done-when lines and test commands. An agent claims one by opening a draft pull request titled with the card key; a claim with no push for a week lapses, and the first pull request merged wins. The board stays the one source of truth, with no second list on GitHub. Both repos got CONTRIBUTING-AGENTS.md and AGENTS.md, the rules for agents: one card per pull request, tests pass, no secrets, CI or release scripts. Feature requests get a template in docs/specs. Three cards are open to start: the browser's first pull request, the Mac app's first pull request, and a Yui Lines parser in Go. Next: a weekly routine prompt for each platform.

title: Talk about a setting, designed: change your agent by talking
body: Step 1 of 2. Chris, Sep 25: "Would it be cool if I could just bring in a certain setting or piece of markdown or whatever setting the agent has into context and then chat about it and have it updated itself." Every item in Controls (the personality, a memory, a skill, a schedule) gets a Talk about this button. The chat opens with that item as a chip above the composer. Say what you want, and the agent proposes the change as a before and after: lines it would drop struck out, new lines highlighted. One tap applies it, through the same path a hand edit in Controls takes, so your Mac checks it, logs it and keeps the old copy. Keep it as is writes nothing. Keys never reach the agent, and only the owner can do this. The spec is at /developers/talk-about and the mock runs in the playground (demo=talk-about). Step 2 builds it in the app, after Controls itself.
