title: Agent controls, designed: change what your agent is made of
body: Step 1 of 2. Chris, Sep 25: "I definitely want just basic crud access to a lot of this stuff." The drawer gets a Controls tab for the agent you are talking to: its personality, its memory, its skills, its schedules, and which model and tools it runs on. Edit the personality and save, forget one memory, switch a skill off or delete it, pause a schedule or run it now. A change goes straight to the machine the agent runs on, with no chat turn in between, and every delete asks first. Keys and tokens never leave that machine; they are not even listed. Only the owner sees Controls, never someone an agent is shared with. The spec is at /developers/controls and the mock runs in the playground (demo=controls). Step 2 builds it in the app.

title: Taps answer at once, and a long thread scrolls smooth
body: Chris, Sep 25: "I am not getting ultra smoothness when I click around. Things feel delayed. Very efficient like Telegram." We measured first, on a 500-message thread in the simulator. Opening it took over three seconds, a tap on a choice took more than a second to show, and every change to the thread redrew all 500 rows. The fixes: each row now knows when it hasn't changed and skips its redraw; what the thread reads on every pass (which rows show, which bubble wears the reaction, the pages) is worked out once per change instead of once per row; markdown is parsed once per message; a long thread draws its newest 60 rows and adds more as you scroll up; and dragging the drawer only redraws the drawer. The look is the same, light and dark. Warm thread open went from about 3 s to under 350 ms, a choice tap from 1.4 s to 58 ms, a reaction from 300 ms to 29 ms, a sent bubble from 2.4 s to 145 ms, and scroll hitches from 63 to under 2 ms per second. Real phone numbers come in through the app's own perf log once the build is out. Rides the next build.
short: Thread open 3 s to under 350 ms, taps under 100 ms, scroll hitches near zero. Same look.

title: The build-ready message reads like a changelog for people
short: When a new build is ready, the message lists what you can now do, in plain words.
body: The message that says a new build is ready used to read like a git log: five pages, one per commit, full of ids. It now finds each change's own entry, titles each page with what a person can do, and folds the builder-only work into one last page. For build 96 the deck went from five pages of code talk to three pages: the hold menu, markdown, and builders. There is no screen to show, the message is text.

title: A deck in the chat is as tall as its page
body: Chris, on build 96: "there's too much random white space here and I would love for this component to look a little more similar to how it does on the full screen version." His screenshot was an inline deck on a four-line page with half a card of nothing above the arrows. The pager in the chat had a fixed height of 380 to 440 points, whatever the page said. Now every page is measured before it shows, and the card is as tall as the page showing, up to a cap past which a very long page scrolls inside it. It grows and shrinks with a spring as you page, and the arrows sit right under the last line. The pages themselves are drawn the way full screen draws them: the same big headline, the quieter body and the numbered points. A new test pages a four-page deck with a short page, a long one and a list, in light and dark, and checks the gap above the arrows on every page and that the card grows for the long page and shrinks back after. Rides the next build.
short: The inline deck fits the page showing and uses the full-screen type, so no more half-empty card.

title: Full-screen pages never come up blank
body: Chris, on build 96: "Sometimes I come to these pages and they don't come back." His screenshot was a full-screen deck with its page bars and arrows around an empty page. A story page's words waited for a signal that the page had arrived before they came on, and the paging view does not always send it. Now the page showing always has its words; the signal only decides which way they slide in from. A new test pages a deck to its end, opens it full screen, closes it, opens it again and swipes and taps both ways, checking the title and body are on screen every time, in light and in dark with Reduce Motion. Rides the next build.
short: The page showing always has its words now, even when the paging view skips its arrival signal.

title: Typing keeps up, even on a long thread
body: Chris, on build 96: holding backspace went slow, and a double space was slow to make the period. The cause: every key you typed made the whole chat redraw itself, every message above included. Now the words you type belong to the composer alone. A key redraws the text field and the little / and @ hints, and nothing else; the Send button swaps in on your first letter without touching the thread. On a simulated thread of 241 messages with cards in it, a key used to take 177 ms to show (375 ms at the slow end) and a fast run of backspaces lost 34 of 49 presses. Now a key shows on the next frame most of the time, the slow end is 62 to 113 ms, and every press lands. The chat redrew 33 times while typing before, zero times now. Rides the next build.
short: A key redraws only the composer now: 177 ms to about one frame on a 241-message thread, and backspace never drops a press.

title: The MCP server and Telegram read Yui Lines like the app again
body: Two copies of the Yui Lines parser had gone quietly stale. The MCP server that lets Claude, ChatGPT and other MCP hosts put screens on your phone, and the Telegram renderer, each carry a copy of the site's parser. When agent tables and app restyles arrived, the parser split into three files, but the scripts that copy it still took one. So the MCP server refused query, put, theme app and the new shapes diagrams as unknown lines, and Telegram pushed them all behind Open in Yui. Both copy scripts now follow the parser's imports and bring the whole set, so the next file it grows comes along on its own. The MCP server is redeployed and its live test, 106 of 106 checks, now sends a theme app, a table, a put, a query and a shapes diagram in one screen and sees them accepted. Telegram draws a shapes diagram as words: the title, the labels in order with arrows between them, and the caption. A query opens in Yui, since the tables live on the phone, and table and put lines send nothing. 73 of 73 Telegram checks. Nothing changes in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/telegram.

title: Shared agents in the app: Hi Maya, Shared by Sam, and a clean goodbye
body: The app side of sharing an agent. A person you invite opens Yui to Hi Maya. Sam set these up for you., their agents underneath in the looks you picked, and one plain line: these agents run on Sam's computer, which keeps your conversations, and other people Sam invites never see them. There is no Add agent on an account that was given its agents. A shared agent's settings say Shared by Sam and offer only what is theirs to change: notifications, and its place in the list. If the agent stops passing the safe-to-share rules it reads Paused by its owner, and messages wait. On your side, every agent's settings now say Safe to share, or Not safe to share and why, in plain words: it has a shell on your computer. Inviting someone is one screen from Yui: who, which safe agents, the look, what each says first, and whether to keep it as a template; Invite runs the scripts and hands back the link. Taking an agent back sends their phone a silent push, so it leaves the list at once; if the thread was open it closes with Basil is no longer shared with you. Thirty days later the old thread is deleted. Two gaps closed too: photos now work both ways in a shared thread, each kept in that person's own folder, and replies are fitted to the client's own phone, not yours. Rides the next build.
short: Invited people see who set their agents up, Shared by in settings, a clean revoke, and Safe to share on your side.

title: Shapes that move
body: Chris, on build 96: generated pictures look fine but cost compute for every little idea; he wanted simple vector drawings that show a complex idea fast, in the chat with a caption. Now an agent writes a few lines and the phone draws a small diagram: circles, boxes, pills, dots, soft blobs, labels, lines, arrows and curves. They come on one after another in the order of the lines, drawing themselves on, springing up, gliding, or gently pulsing on the part that matters, then a caption says what it means. With no positions they line up in a row and the arrows find their ends, so a flow is five short lines. Colors come from the agent's look, Reduce Motion shows the finished drawing, and nothing is rendered off the phone. Agents learn it in channel guide v22: asked how a heat pump works, the new guide drew it; the old one wrote a paragraph. Live in the web playground; the iPhone draws it on main and reaches the phone with the next build.

title: The release timeline, live from the board
body: Where the next version stands used to be a list Yui typed in chat, out of date by the next card that moved. Now it is built from the board. The board export carries the release: the open YUI-SHIP card, or the last one that landed, and the cards it waits on. From that and the build list, one panel: how many cards landed, the cards done, running or queued, the four ship steps (tests, one upload, VALID, what to try goes out), and everything on the app's main branch since the last TestFlight build. Right now it shows 0.2.0 shipped as build 122 and the changes on main for the next one. Try it at /playground?demo=release, or from the tile on Builds; it redraws with every board sync. How it works, and how it will patch in place on the phone with no agent turn, is in the new spec at /developers/release. The phone side is YUI-105: the panel at the top of the war room.

title: Yui now times itself: speed numbers from real phones, every day
body: The speed budget written earlier today is now measured. On the phone, nine moments are timed from your tap to the frame that shows the answer: a key appearing, your bubble after Send, an agent's message landing, a page swipe settling, full screen opening, a thread opening (first and later), launch and coming back. Each shows by name in Instruments and is timed on the phone's own clock. Memory is sampled every 30 seconds, and Apple's daily MetricKit report adds hangs, scroll hitches, memory peaks and crash stacks. It all travels as numbers only: no message text, no names, nothing you wrote. A new table, yui_perf, keeps each person's rows to themselves and their own agents, at most 500 a day, gone after 90 days. Yui (the agent) reads them into a daily report: p50 and p95 against the budget, what got slower than the build before, and the worst hang stacks, matched to code. The war room has a Speed panel under Builds (the shot uses sample numbers until real ones come in), and the morning briefing gets one line only when something got worse. Test builds have a Speed switch in Settings that shows the last keystroke time and the frame rate. What the build taught is in section 10 of the speed budget. Rides the next build.
short: Nine moments timed on real phones, numbers only, a daily report and a Speed panel that flags what got slower.

title: What fast means for Yui, in milliseconds
body: Chris asked for Yui to feel as quick as Telegram, and for numbers Yui can watch. Before any fix, a yardstick. The new speed budget names seven moments people feel (a key reaching the screen, a sent message showing, an agent's message landing, a swipe, a full-screen open, a thread open, launch) and gives each a target: one frame for typing and sending, under 100 ms for a tap, 300 ms to open a thread. It sets budgets for hangs, scroll hitches and memory too, based on Apple's hitch and hang guidance. The phone will send numbers only, never what anyone wrote, into a table only the owner can read. A daily report compares each build with the one before, and the morning briefing speaks up only when something got slower. The war room gets a Speed panel, drawn here with sample numbers from presets the app already has. Step 2 (YUI-102) builds it into the app.

title: Ask any agent to restyle Yui, in the app
body: Say "make Yui feel like autumn" to any agent you own and it answers with one line. Yui draws a card: two small phones, Yui as it is now beside Yui in autumn, and a Light / Dark switch that flips both. If a color had to move so text stays readable, one line says so. Nothing changes until you tap Use autumn. Then the app fades into the new look and the card leaves Undo, one step back. Keep mine closes the card, and a newer offer retires an older one. The look covers everything that is nobody's thread: Yui's own thread, the sheets, Settings and sign-in. Every other agent keeps its own look in its thread, so you still know who you are talking to; Settings > Look has a switch to put the whole app in one look, and Back to Yui's look is always one tap. The look is saved to your account and cached on the phone so the first frame is right. Agents shared with you by someone else can never restyle your app, and phones too old to show the card never see the line. It rides the next Yui release.

title: Share an agent with a client, and take it back
body: The plumbing for sharing is live. You pick agents for an invite, each in a look and with a first message. The person signs in and the agent is in their list, dressed the way you picked, its first message waiting. Each person gets their own thread, and you never read it; neither does anyone else you invite. Take the agent back and it is gone from their app on the next open, and the agent can no longer read or write that thread. Safety is checked three times. The agent's computer reports how it is set up with every heartbeat, and only an agent with no shell, no files, no reach into the rest of the computer, no shared memory and a model reached through an API counts as safe to share. The grant script refuses anything else and says which rule failed, the database refuses it again, and the agent checks itself before every turn for someone who is not its owner. Tested on the simulator with a made-up client: Penny shows up in pink, says hi, and after a revoke she is gone. Next in the app: the invite screen for you, and a Shared by line for them.

title: Invite a client and their agents are already there, on paper and in the playground
body: Invites are how new people get into Yui right now. This step writes down what an invite can carry: a set of agents, each in a look you pick, each with a first message. The person signs in with Apple and their agent list is already filled, with a new message waiting from each one. They get their own thread with each agent. They can mute one or move it in the list, but not rename it or delete it. Take an agent back and it leaves their app at once. The harder part is safety. Most agents on a developer's computer can run any command and read any file, which is fine for their owner and never fine for someone else. So an agent can be shared only if it passes five rules: its own profile, no shell and no files outside a sandbox, no reach into the rest of the computer, nothing carried from one person to the next, and a model reached through an API. The grant script refuses any other agent, the database refuses it again, and the agent checks itself before every turn for someone who is not its owner. Try both sides in the playground: making the invite, and the first open. The app gets it in a later release.

title: Yui 0.2.0: every agent gets a home
body: Yui 0.2.0 is on TestFlight as build 122, the first real release after a week of hourly builds. Apple started turning uploads away, so we held TestFlight, finished a set of features, ran the full test pass and uploaded once. Drag right on any chat and the agent's drawer slides out: Home, Review, Controls and About. Agents fill it themselves, with asks in Review, a Backlog and one-tap Shortcuts. Screens update where they sit: a timer, a score or a status line changes in place instead of arriving again, and those quiet updates don't buzz your phone. Full-screen pages read like a story, one idea per page. Agents can draw a quick sketch of a window, a phone or a chat bubble. You can type on a screen that keeps a composer. Needs you is one block per ask, the buttons under the question. Anything this build can't draw yet shows as one Update chip, not red lines. And Settings now ends with About this build: version, build, channel, commit and date, tap to copy. A Yui Dev copy for test links installs beside it, so the two never get mixed up. Install or update it at https://testflight.apple.com/join/ykrYHwet

title: Group threads: the plumbing is live
body: Yesterday we wrote down how a group of agents should behave. Today the database and the agent side do it. A group has its own thread, with a lead who answers anything you don't address. Your message goes to the agents you @, and only to them; the others see it on their next turn. When one agent @s another, the ask goes through on a budget: three handoffs and eight agent turns per message by default. Past that the ask is held until you say Let it or Stop, and Stop also cancels every handoff nobody has picked up yet. Each agent still reads only its own messages. What it knows of the rest of the group is a short quote above each ask and one line per message since its last turn, and only while it is a member. The agents' guide got a Groups section: answer only your part, hand work on in one plain sentence, never bounce it back. We tested it on three new cases and it passed all three. The database side passed 69 checks against the live project. The app's side, the New group sheet and the thread itself, is next and ships in a later release.
short: Group threads work under the hood: who answers, handoffs on a budget, Let it and Stop. The app is next.

title: Group threads: several agents in one conversation, on paper and in the playground
body: You can already @ another agent from any thread. The next step is a thread with several agents in it, and before building it we wrote down how it should behave. The rule for who answers is simple: the agent you @ answers, and if you @ nobody, the group's lead does. Nobody jumps in on a message that wasn't for them. When one agent asks another for help, the thread shows it as its own row, both faces and the ask, and every agent keeps its own colors. Agents can keep handing work on, but on a budget: one message of yours buys a few handoffs and at most eight agent turns. Past that, the ask waits for you with two buttons, Let it and Stop here, and a Stop button sits on the working rows the whole time. The spec also covers how a group is stored, why no agent can read another agent's messages even in a group, and what older copies of the app see. Try the mock in the playground: Coach plans race week, asks Sage for a wind-down, and Sage's ask to Quill hits the guard. The app gets it in a later release.
short: Group threads, written down and mocked: who answers, how a handoff shows, and a loop guard you control.

title: Connect your tools: the plan, and a flow you can try
body: Agents get useful when they can reach your calendar, your mail and your CRM. This step writes down how that will work in Yui, and turns the connect screens into a flow you can run. A connector is the tool's own MCP server, the open standard agents use to call tools: Google now runs one for Calendar and one for Gmail, and HubSpot runs one too. You sign in once, on Google's or HubSpot's own page, never in Yui. Before that, each tool gets a consent step that says what it allows in plain words instead of scope names: Calendar can see your events and find a time, and adding one is a separate ask later; Gmail can read, label and write drafts, and has no send button, so every draft waits for you; HubSpot sees only what your own login can see. The sign-in stays with your agent on your own computer, never in the app and never in a Yui database, and you can switch a tool off from the drawer or on Google and HubSpot directly. The sign-in buttons come from the agent after the flow, because a real sign-in link is made fresh for each person. Nothing signs in yet: the buttons open the spec. Real sign-in is step 2, and it needs a Google Cloud project and a HubSpot app registered first. Try it in the playground under Flow: connect your tools, and read it at /developers/connectors.
short: How your agent will use your calendar, mail and CRM: plain-words consent, then one sign-in each.

title: See it catches up with 0.2.0
body: Every change you can see gets a place on See it, and five from the next release had none. Now a Yui 0.2.0 group sits near the top of /mockups: each agent's drawer, the menu word that lets an agent fill it, screens that update in place, the app drawing sketches, and one Update chip instead of red lines for anything your copy of Yui can't draw yet. Where the web can draw it, the phone on the page is live, so you can tap the leg day timeline or the sketch; the drawer itself is shown with real captures from the simulator. Each one is labelled In Yui 0.2.0 until that build is on TestFlight. The site group also got its two newest pages: Yui's values and the shared type scale.

title: Meet Yui: an onboarding interview that suggests your first agents
body: A new person's first minute in Yui is now written down, and you can run it. Yui asks three quick things on full screens: your name, how much you know about AI on a 1 to 5 slider, and what you want help with, in taps and then in your own words. Each answer changes what comes next. Brand new gets a one-page answer to what an agent is. Four and up gets asked if you already run one. Pick get fit and eat better and Yui suggests Coach, a trainer, and Basil, a nutritionist; get organized gets Penny, an assistant; learning something gets Quill, a study buddy. Each comes with a look the app already has. The last page is honest about today: Yui draws the screens and the agent runs on your own computer, so it says how to connect one. It is a saved flow, so any agent can send `flow onboarding`, and it is in the library. Try it in the playground under Flow: meet yui. The app runs it on first launch after 0.2.0.
short: Yui's first-run interview: three quick questions, then two starter agents picked for you.

Light mode, step 5 of 9: What do you want help with? Chips for Get fit, Eat better, Get organized, Learn something and Type your own, then Done.

title: Agents keep data on your phone: tables
body: An agent can now keep a workout log, today's macros or a small CRM, and draw it any time. Three new words in Yui Lines do it. table create makes a table with typed columns (text, number, date, on or off). put writes one row: with a key it updates that row, without one it adds a row, so a log just appends. query draws the rows as a table, a list, a chart or one big number, and it stays live: send a put and every view on screen redraws. A query can filter (Day=today), sort, and total by group, so "best set per lift" or "protein by day" is one line. Dates like today and today-7 are read on the phone, so the agent never has to know yours. The rows stay on the phone. The agent sees them only when you tick a box in a list or tap Send on the rows you choose to share. This step is the spec and the web version: try the three starters in the playground under Agent tables, send the put in the agent line and watch the views change. Rows you add stay in your browser until you reset them. The iPhone app gets the same store next.

images.alt: Workout log in the playground: a line chart of squat top sets rising from 215 to 235 pounds over a week, and a table of the best set per lift with reps and set counts.
Macros in light mode: a big number reading 1,090 kcal today with a spark line, a table of today's three meals with calories and protein, and a bar chart of protein by day.
A simple CRM: a table of open deals with stage, value and next date, a bar chart of pipeline value by stage, and a checklist where two deals are ticked as won.

title: Agents fill the drawer
body: The drawer from YUI-54 filled itself: pinned screens, open questions, About. Now the agent can add to it too, with one new word in Yui Lines. menu review@dana "Invite Dana to the beta?" puts a card in Review, under the thread's own questions, and counts on the menu button. menu backlog@deload "Deload week plan" sub=drafting lists what the agent is working on for you, in a new Backlog section on Home. menu shortcut "Start the workout" adds a one-tap shortcut above the host's commands; a tap sends it as your message, and one that ends in a space, like say="Log a meal: ", fills the composer for you to finish. menu done dana takes one out, and you can hold any item to remove it. The lines draw nothing in the chat. Three lists, 20 items each, no nesting, so no agent can crowd the drawer or restyle it. A tapped review or backlog item goes back to the agent, which answers with the screen. In the eval, asked for a one-tap breakfast log, the agent added the shortcut on its own; tapped on its deload item, it sent the plan and marked the item draft ready. Cards got +fold too (Chris's round-4 note: cards you can open): title, sub and a line of body, and a tap opens the rest in place. Spec in YL.md, 27 new conformance vectors, and all five parsers (JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin, Rust) pass them. Rides the 0.2.0 build; older phones drop the lines quietly.

title: Cron failures go to Yui, not to your chat
body: Chris sent a screenshot of his Yui thread: a raw alert that a weekly job had failed, with a Python traceback in it. He did not want those. There is nothing for him to do with one, and it would come back to Yui anyway. So now every scheduled job Yui runs without an agent goes through a small guard script. When the job works, its message goes out exactly as before. When it fails or runs too long, the guard says nothing in the chat. It logs the failure, and it opens one card on Yui's board for that job, or adds a note to the card that is already open. Yui's lane driver reads that log every half hour and fixes the script or hands it to whoever owns the broken part. Chris hears about it only when the same job has failed three runs in a row and it is holding up Yui work, as one short line, never a traceback. The failing job itself, a weekly report that crashed on an older Python, was fixed first. A script on the Mac, so nothing to screenshot.

title: Week of Sep 21: from a first build to build 96, then a pause for 0.2.0
body: Yui's first week in public. On Monday there was a pitch and a roadmap. The first TestFlight build went out Wednesday, and by Friday the app had reached build 96: Sign in with Apple, every preset drawn native, decks and full-screen plans, reactions, replies, @mentions, slash commands, games, a war room with a timeline you can reorder, and a drawer for each agent. Agents from outside Hermes can talk in Yui now: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, LangGraph, CrewAI, n8n and any A2A agent. The site grew a public board, a changelog by build, See it, the library and Thoughts. The honest problem: we shipped too often. Five uploads in one day, and Apple started turning builds away. So TestFlight is paused except for crash fixes, and the next build will be one real release, 0.2.0, with the drawer as each agent's home and screens that refresh in place. After that, the MVP test: a stranger goes from invite to first screen with no help.

A Yui reply in light mode: a card, then one small chip reading Update Yui to see this

title: Screens your Yui can't draw yet turn into words
body: Chris sent a screenshot with a question: something looks broken. Yui had answered with a drawing, a sketch of the INT-7 ask with the old buttons crossed out and the new ones highlighted. His phone runs build 96, and sketches arrived in build 104, so every line of the drawing showed as a red unknown preset with the raw lines under it. Nothing crashed, but it read as broken, and he was right. Three fixes. The relay now knows which build each phone runs: the app already says it in every request it makes, so this works for the phones out there today. The plugin checks that build before a reply leaves the Mac: anything the phone can't draw goes out as plain words, so the same answer on build 96 reads as a short list, the old option struck through and the new one in bold. Inside a deck it becomes a page of points. And the agent is told which screens to skip on that phone. For the next release, the app itself folds anything it can't draw into one quiet Update Yui chip instead of raw lines. Tested live against the relay and in the simulator, light and dark.
short: Anything your Yui can't draw yet arrives as plain words or one Update chip, never raw lines.

images.alt: A Yui reply in light mode: a card that draws, then one small chip reading Update Yui to see this, and no raw lines
The same reply in dark mode, the card and one Update Yui to see this chip

title: Yui for macOS has a brief, open for contributors
body: Chris wants Yui on the Mac too. It is now a written plan anyone can pick up. The Mac app ships under the same app record as the phone, so it is the same account and the same Sign in with Apple, with no new roles and no new tokens. It is a real Mac app, not the phone app in a window: the agent drawer becomes a sidebar that stays open, Return sends, Command-K switches agents, and the stage opens in its own window that can go full screen. A translation table covers every screen: most draw exactly as on the phone, the camera and mic work the Mac way, a running timer lives in the menu bar instead of the lock screen, and anything that needs the phone says Open on your iPhone instead of breaking. Four pull requests in order, each with its tests on macOS. The first needs no account: the Mac target builds and opens a demo chat. Signing and release stay with us, so no keys in any pull request. A spec, so nothing to screenshot in the app yet.

title: Each agent gets a drawer
body: The top-left button used to open a list of your agents, and nothing else. Now each agent has a home. Drag right on the chat and a drawer follows your finger out from the left. It stops short, so the chat still peeks out on the right; tap that sliver, drag back left or hit the X to close it. On a screen, a drag right pages back to the chat first, so it never fights the pager. Chris picked this layout from three mocks: Peek and tabs. Home has your pinned screens (the workout you open every day), what's next for you, and the screens in this thread. Review holds everything waiting on you, and each ask opens in place with its buttons, so you answer right there. Controls is where the agent's name, look and notifications live, with room for its soul, memory, skills and schedules next (YUI-70). About is saved for a page about the agent, once hosts can describe themselves. The agent you're talking to sits at the bottom. Tap it and your other agents spring up above it, with Add an agent. Reduce Motion swaps the slide for a fade. It rides the next build with YUI-70.

images.alt: The drawer open in dark mode over the chat: Wizard in big type, tabs Home, Review with a 1, Controls, About; a pinned workout tile, Pick a drawer under Next up for you, the Leg day screen, and Wizard, Online at the bottom
The Review tab in light mode: 1 thing is waiting on you, the Pick a drawer ask opened in place with its context and the buttons Calm, Playful and Peek
The switcher sprung up from the bottom in dark mode: Yui, Coach, Wizard with a check, Counsel offline, Nova, then Add an agent and Edit list

title: Screens update in place instead of piling up
body: An agent can now give a piece of a screen a name and change it later, across replies. A timer, a score or a status line updates where it sits instead of arriving again as a new screen. Replies that only change something already on screen don't buzz your phone. The war room uses it first: a refresh patches the numbers on its page rather than sending the whole page again. All five parsers (JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin, Rust) share ten new test cases. It reaches the app with 0.2.0.

title: The library: every screen and flow, live and searchable
body: yuigui.com/developers/library puts every screen an agent can send on one page: 35 tiles, each a live phone you can tap, with the line that draws it, what it is for and a few tags. Copy the line, or open it in the playground. The Flows tab draws each saved flow as its Mermaid chart, the same text GitHub draws, with a Run it button into the playground. Search runs in the browser over names, purposes, tags and the lines themselves. Agents get the same list at /library.json, with a pointer in llms.txt, so an agent can look up a screen or a flow and send it as is. A check fails the build step when a preset has no tile or an example stops parsing. Checked light and dark at phone and desktop width: nothing clipped, nothing wider than the screen.

images.alt: The library page on a wide screen: a search bar, Screens and Flows tabs, and a row of live phones for timer, ask and choose, each with its line, tags, Copy and Open in playground.
The Flows tab in dark mode: the client website intake flow drawn as a Mermaid chart, with a Run it button beside it.
Searching the library for intake: three screens and one flow match, and only those tiles stay on the page.

title: Yui in the browser has a brief, open for contributors
body: Yui in a browser tab is now a written plan anyone can pick up. The spec says what it is: Sign in with Apple, the same relay the phone uses, and the playground's renderer, so an agent cannot tell a tab from the phone. A translation table says what each screen does in a browser: haptics dropped, camera and mic through the browser, timers kept by the clock so a background tab stays right, push later through Web Push, and anything a tab cannot do says Open on your iPhone instead of breaking. No new roles and no new tokens. The first pull request needs no account at all: a thread page drawn from a recorded thread, checked tap for tap against the playground. It is listed on the contribute page as open for contributors. A spec, so nothing to screenshot yet.

title: The site reads like the app now
body: Build 96 made the app type-led: big clear titles, short bodies, nothing cut off. The site now reads the same way. One type scale runs every page: the same title, section and card heading sizes everywhere, where before there were nine. Headings sit tight instead of borrowing the body's loose line height, and they wrap in balanced lines, so a title no longer leaves one word alone. Reading text stops at about 70 characters a line on a wide screen, down from as many as 170. On a phone, small print is at least 16px. Checked at phone and desktop width on all 18 pages in the menu: nothing clipped, nothing wider than the screen.

images.alt: The Get Yui page on a phone, before on the left and after on the right. After, the step title wraps as two even lines and the headings sit closer to their text.
The Shipped page on a wide screen, before and after. After, the headings are on the shared scale and the intro stops at a comfortable line length.

title: Asks sit with what they ask about
body: Chris's feedback on the war room: every ask was two cards, the context on top and the buttons in a separate box under it, so the answer looked cut off from what it was about. Now each ask is one card: the card's tag, its name and the context, then the question and the buttons. Two answers ride every ask, always last. Not yet is for when the ask assumes you already did something, like a browser step. The card stays waiting and nothing restarts. You decide hands the call back, and the agent picks the option it recommends and goes. Under the hood, choose and pick take tag, title and body, in the app, on the web and in the MCP App. Phones on an older build still get the two-card layout until the next build.

The same asks in light mode

title: Flows, written in Mermaid
body: Plan mode walks you through a few screens in a straight line. Flows add the map. A flow is a Mermaid flowchart, the same text GitHub draws as a chart: each box carries one screen, and the labels on the arrows are conditions on your earlier answers. Pick Shop and the intake asks about products and payments; pick Landing page and it skips the page list. The same step reads 4 of 9 on one branch and 4 of 6 on the other. Back walks the path you took, the review lists only what you answered on it, and the agent gets one event with the answers and the path. An agent can send a flow inline or run a saved one by name, like flow website-intake. Three starter flows come from real work: a client website intake, scoping a project yourself, and a workout check-in. All three run in the playground, and a browser test takes every branch of every one. This step is the spec and the web runtime; the app runs flows next. Spec: /developers/flows.

After Shop, light: step 4 of 9, How many products? on a slider from 1 to 500
After Landing page instead, light: step 4 of 6, What should a visitor do first? Call, Book, Buy, Sign up, Read

title: The admin console, scoped
body: Yui will need people who run it from the top, so we wrote down who they are before building anything. Five roles: the owner, a super user or two, admins for the daily work, support who can look things up but change nothing alone, and a company's own admin who runs only their people and their default agents. A table says what each role can touch: invites, accounts, the kill switch and limits, feature flags, announcements, feedback, usage numbers and an audit log. Next to each control is what exists today and what is missing. Our recommendation is an Admin section inside the app, not a web console: Sign in with Apple already works there, and the site has no login to secure. A role is a row checked on every request, never inside the token, and anything destructive asks again with Face ID and a fresh Apple sign-in. Admins never read messages: the admin API has no way to return them, and the doc lists exactly what is visible. It ends with three phases and six cards to pick from. No build yet, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/admin.

title: The app draws
body: Feedback on build 96 asked Yui to draw a little window with some things crossed out and others highlighted, instead of explaining in words. The app now draws sketches itself. An agent sends a frame, a window, a phone or a chat bubble, and a few rows: some struck out, some highlighted, some greyed, some drawn as buttons, blank ones as filler, each with an optional short note and an arrow. One line splits it into a before and an after. In the chat a sketch sits on a card. On a full-screen page it is the page's picture: the frame comes on first, then each row, then the headline and the words. A sketch with no page before it is a page that is only the drawing. The spec gained that rule, so agents can put a sketch right under a page line, and all five parsers and the web playground follow it. VoiceOver reads each drawn row with its marks, so a crossed-out line is read as crossed out. Lands with the next build.

images.alt: A full-screen page, dark: a chat bubble drawn before and after, the old line with a card id struck through ('an id tells you nothing'), the new line in plain words highlighted ('plain words'), and under it the headline 'No card or feedback ids'
The same page in light mode
The next page: a phone drawn with 'Build 97 is ready', a 'Got it' button struck through ('does nothing') and an 'Install' button highlighted ('does the thing'), headline 'Every button does something'
In the chat, dark: the same drawing on the deck's card, and a small window sketch on its own card below with 'Hold menu fits' highlighted and an id struck and greyed
The drawn page at the largest accessibility text size

title: Yui Lines in Rust
body: Yui Lines now has a fifth parser, in Rust. It is a crate with no dependencies: no regex library and no serde, only the standard library, with a small JSON reader of its own for custom lines. Each rule of the JavaScript parser is ported line by line, with the pattern it replaces written next to it. It passes all 445 shared test vectors in 25 files, read straight from the spec folder, and spec/conformance/run-all.sh now runs it next to JavaScript, Python and Kotlin. We also fed it 35,000 random documents and compared every result with the JavaScript parser: whole parses, streams cut into random chunks, what opens full screen, which pages can talk, and every screen with its defaults filled in. No differences. The README lists the few Unicode edge cases Rust strings cannot hold. The Developers page lists all five parsers. Go or C# is a good first contribution.

images.alt: The Parsers section of the Developers page on yuigui.com, light: JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin and now Rust, 'parsers/rust. A crate with no dependencies, standard library only.'
The same Parsers section in dark mode, five parsers listed with Rust last

title: AG-UI agents in Yui
body: Agents served over AG-UI can come into Yui by their URL. AG-UI is the protocol agents use to talk to the app in front of them, and Microsoft Agent Framework, CopilotKit, Mastra and Pydantic AI all speak it. The new bridge makes Yui that app. Each message you send is one run, and the bridge keeps the conversation, since AG-UI servers remember nothing between runs. Screens are a tool the agent calls, yui_show: the run stops there, the screen goes to your phone, and your tap goes back as the tool's answer. That is AG-UI's own way of waiting on a person, so nothing is bent to fit. We ran Agent Framework's own AG-UI endpoint on a small local model, with instructions that never mention Yui, through live Yui on a test account: asked for a drink, it called yui_show with a Tea or Coffee picker on the first try, took the tap back, remembered it the next turn, and a crash in the middle of a turn still got one answer, 16 of 16 checks. The bridge reuses the A2A bridge's Yui side, so delivery works the same. One open question for Chris: whether Yui should also read A2UI, Google's UI format, which Agent Framework can send over AG-UI. Our take is not now. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/agui.

title: Full-screen pages tell a story
body: Feedback on build 96 held up a long answer read as pages: a card inside the full screen, a title cut off at "with the…", and a bullet list split across three pages. Now full screen is the whole stage. There is no card on it. Each page carries one idea: every list item gets its own page, and prose comes a sentence or two at a time. The headline is set big and sized to its words, so a five-word idea fills the screen, and it never breaks a word. The body is a second, quieter voice. A thin bar per page runs across the top. Words spring on when a page arrives and drift off when it leaves; with Reduce Motion they only fade. Titles stop after a whole clause, and a lead-in that ends in a colon ends in "…" so the next page picks it up. Decks, plans and walkthroughs all open this way, and host reports no longer repeat a title with "(2/3)". Each page leaves room for a picture. Drawn ones come next. Lands with the next build.

title: Agents can draw now
body: From TestFlight feedback: "Yui should be pretty good at just drawing different stuff so we don't even have to generate images or screenshots." Now an agent can draw a small picture in a few lines. A sketch is a little window, phone or chat bubble with rows in it. A row can be struck out, highlighted, greyed, drawn as a button, or left blank as filler, and a short note beside the frame points at it with an arrow. One line in the middle splits it into before and after. It sends nothing back; it is there to show instead of tell. Agents learn it in channel guide v18, next to long reports. In the eval, the old guide answered "show me the difference" with a table and words; the new one drew it both times. Live in the web playground and in the MCP App now. The iPhone view comes next.

A small browser window for a pottery shop's home page: the tagline highlighted to keep, 'Welcome to our website!' struck out, the newsletter button greyed with the note 'move to the footer'

title: Yui's values, written down
body: Feedback on a build-ready deck said it plainly: three cards of split-up text is not what Yui is. The same note named what Yui should be, and those are now eight values on one page: screens, not text bombs; one idea per page; type tells the story; full screen is the whole stage, with no card inside it; draw it, don't describe it; say what is being done, not who did it; nothing cut off mid-sentence; every button does something. Each comes with one example. The agent guide points to them where it teaches long answers, and the build-in-public rules hold progress entries and Thoughts to them. The app work they call for (full-screen pages that tell a story, little drawn windows) is on the board next. Page: /developers/values.

The values page on a phone: the title Yui's values, the intro and the first value, Screens, not text bombs

title: Flue agents in Yui
body: Agents built with Flue, the TypeScript agent framework from the team behind Astro, can come into Yui. Flue adds integrations as channels: you run `flue add channel` and hand the guide it prints to your coding agent. Yui now has that guide, plus a small connector. Your Flue app dials out to Yui, so there is no webhook to expose, and every message you send goes to the agent through Flue's own dispatch. Its answer comes back once, even across a crash. Yui's agent guide goes into the agent's instructions, and that is all it takes to get screens. We ran a Flue agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker its own instructions never asked for, answered the tap, remembered it the next turn, and a crash in the middle of a turn still got one answer, 14 of 14 checks. The connector's Yui side is the same code the A2A bridge runs, now shared. On Cloudflare, where Flue agents usually live, Yui will push turns to the app instead; that waits on the hosted connector. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/adapters.

title: Chat with a screen
short: An agent can keep the composer on one of its screens, so you can type about what is there without going back to the chat.
body: Screens beside the chat are full screen, for reading and tapping, and typing happens in the chat. Now an agent can open a screen up for talk: one line, `>2 talk`, keeps the composer on screen 2. The field says "About screen 2", and what you type there reaches the agent with a first line that names the screen, so it knows you mean the plan on it and can change it in place. Your message shows in the chat with a small "From screen 2" mark that takes you back. `talk off` closes it again, and clearing the screen closes it too. Screens without it stay exactly as they were. The new word is in the spec and in all four parsers (JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin), 419 of 419 test lines in each, and the agent guide teaches it: in two new test turns the agent put a week of runs on a screen with talk on, then changed Thursday in place when asked from that screen. Tested on an iPhone 18 Pro simulator. It rides the next TestFlight build. Spec: /developers/yl.

images.alt: Screen 2 in dark mode with a Week one card and a Runs checklist, and a composer at the bottom that reads About screen 2.
Screen 3 with a Notes list and no composer, only the chat icon and page dots at the bottom.
The chat with Swap Thursday for a swim as the person's message, marked From screen 2 above it, and the agent's answer below.

title: Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Yui
body: Agents built with Microsoft Agent Framework, the successor to AutoGen, can come into Yui. Agent Framework serves an agent over A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs it by its card URL. Two catches. It reads every text in a message as what you said, so the example agent moves Yui's guide into the agent's instructions, its system prompt. And it forgets the thread each turn, so the example keeps one session per thread. We also fixed the bridge: without streaming, Agent Framework sends its answer as a progress note and then finishes with nothing, and the bridge used to drop it. We ran an Agent Framework agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, answered the tap and remembered it the next turn, 10 of 10 checks. We also looked at AG-UI, another way agents talk to apps: Yui can speak it too, with its screens as a tool the agent calls, and that is now its own card. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: CrewAI agents in Yui
body: Agents built with CrewAI can come into Yui. CrewAI can serve an agent over A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs it by its card URL, no change needed. One catch: CrewAI reads every text in a message as the task and drops the labels on them, so Yui's guide would read as part of what you said. The example agent moves the guide into the agent's backstory, which is CrewAI's system prompt. We ran a CrewAI agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, and answered the tap, 9 of 9 checks. Crews you run as a script come in through the webhook bridge instead, and the repo has one. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: n8n workflows in Yui
body: n8n workflows can now put a screen on your phone and wait for your tap. Three ways. A Yui node you drag in after any trigger: Ask and Wait shows a choice, a form or a timer, and the next node gets what you tapped, no AI needed. n8n's AI Agent with its MCP Client Tool pointed at Yui's MCP server, so the agent decides when to ask. And a Webhook trigger behind the webhook bridge, which makes Yui the chat front end of a workflow. We ran all three in a real n8n against live Yui on a test account: a small local model put a lunch picker up and said "You picked Soup for lunch." after the tap, the node handed the tap to the next step, and the webhook answered a hi with a screen, 22 of 22 checks. The node isn't on npm yet. No new app screens, so no screenshots. Guide: /developers/mcp#n8n.

title: The hold menu fits any message
body: Holding a long message used to go wrong: the message ran up under the header, the reactions landed at the bottom and the Reply, Copy, Select text menu sat right on top of them, so you could not tap an emoji. Now the layout is always the same column: reactions on top, the message, the menu underneath, all on screen and never touching. A message too tall for that room lifts as a preview of its top with a soft fade where it is cut. Copy, Select text and the new Share row still take every word. It works for a message at the top of the thread, one at the bottom, your own messages and cards, with a reaction's Remove row, and at large text sizes. Tap anywhere outside, or the preview, to close. Tested on an iPhone 18 Pro and an iPhone 17e in light, dark and the biggest accessibility text we checked. It rides the next TestFlight build.

title: Agent answers read clean
body: Agents and the Hermes gateway often answer in markdown, and Yui used to show the raw stars and backticks: a /status answer read as **Model:** with the marks in it. Agent bubbles now draw it: bold, code on a soft tint, code blocks, bullet and numbered lists, headings and links (only https links tap). Screens written in Yui Lines are untouched, anything malformed stays as written, and your own messages look exactly as you typed them. Copy, Select text and VoiceOver get the plain words, and a long answer still folds into pages. 11 new unit tests, 94 in all, and the phone runs pass in light and dark. It rides the next build.

images.alt: Yui chat in light mode: a /status answer with bold labels and the model name in code, then a sample with a bold heading, bullets, a numbered list, a code block and a link
The same chat in dark mode, markdown drawn in the agent's bubbles

title: LangGraph agents in Yui
body: Agents built with LangGraph can come into Yui. LangGraph's own server, the one langgraph dev runs and LangSmith deployments use, speaks A2A for every graph, so the A2A bridge pairs a graph by its card URL. One catch: that server keeps only one text part per message and drops the labels on parts, so Yui's guide could vanish. For LangGraph the bridge now sends the guide and any taps as data, which LangGraph hands the graph as state. A graph declares two keys and can read Yui's guide and the person's taps. We ran a scripted graph, no model, through live Yui: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, and read the tap from its data, 12 of 12 checks. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: Meta's Muse Spark in Yui
body: Muse Spark, Meta's model, can come into Yui as a model. The model bridge has a Meta preset: set MODEL_API_KEY, pair with --server meta (or muse), and it uses muse-spark-1.3 unless you pick another. There is no way to plug into the Meta AI app itself, so this goes through Meta's Model API, which copies OpenAI's and is in public preview for US developers. Where it differs, the bridge copes: a bad key, an empty balance and a model the key can't use each say what they are, a message the safety filter blocks says so, a busy server waits as long as Meta asks, and a slow plain answer says to stream instead of retrying. 17 new tests replay those shapes, 65 in all. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. The first live call waits on a Model API key. Spec: /developers/models.

title: The chat never gets stuck shrunk
body: Chris hit a bug on TestFlight: the whole chat shrank behind a border and nothing undid it. The chat steps back only while a screen is really on stage, so a stage whose reply went away now closes itself, and a tap or swipe on the stepped-back chat closes it too. Replies with nothing left to draw no longer leave a lone agent face in the thread. 83 unit tests and the stage, pages, reply and long message UI tests pass in light and dark. It rides the next build.

images.alt: Light: the chat back at full size after a new look closes the screen
Dark: after the war room, the agents sheet and an agent switch, the chat is full size

title: Grok in Yui, two ways
body: Grok can come into Yui as a model, or call Yui as a tool. As a model: the model bridge has a Grok preset. Set XAI_API_KEY, pair with --server grok, and it uses grok-4.7 unless you pick another. xAI's API copies OpenAI's with a few differences: errors come as a code and a message, a bad key comes back as a 400, a team out of credits gets a 403, and reasoning models refuse some arguments. The bridge handles each one, and says out of credits instead of bad key when that is the problem. 11 new tests replay those shapes, 48 in all. As a tool: xAI's Responses API takes remote MCP servers in the request, so a Grok agent can pass Yui's MCP server with a connection token and put screens on your phone. The spec has a request you can copy, with no token in it. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. The first live call waits on an xAI key. Specs: /developers/models and /developers/mcp.

title: Gemini in Yui, two ways
body: Gemini can come into Yui as a model or as an agent. As a model: the model bridge has a Gemini preset. Set GEMINI_API_KEY, then pair with --server gemini --model gemini-2.5-flash. Google's endpoint copies OpenAI's API with a few differences: model names come back as models/..., errors come wrapped in a list, a bad key comes back as a 400. The bridge handles each one, with 11 new tests that replay those shapes. As an agent: agents built with Google's Agent Development Kit speak A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs them by their card. We ran a real ADK agent on a local model through Yui: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker from Yui's guide, and answered the tap, 9 of 9 checks. The example shows how an ADK agent passes Yui's guide to its model. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. One live call to Gemini itself waits on a free AI Studio key. Specs: /developers/models and /developers/a2a.

title: Yui screens in Telegram
body: The insurance policy is real now. If the app is not around, an agent's Yui screen can still reach you in Telegram. Questions become buttons under the message, and a tap goes back to the agent as the exact line the phone sends, changed answers and all. Lists, cards, stats and tables become formatted text. A timer, a chart, a deck or a form goes behind one Open in Yui button, which opens the whole screen in a Telegram Mini App at yuigui.com/tg, in the chat's own colors. Every preset is covered, none dropped: 62 unit checks, and all 61 playground screens drawn in Telegram's dark and light themes in a real browser, with taps checked through both ways back to the bot. No bot runs it yet: that needs its own Telegram bot and comes next. Spec: /developers/telegram.

title: No more text bombs
body: Chris opened a build ping and got a wall: the whole commit message for the A2A bridge, test counts and all, in one bubble. That is the chatbot experience Yui exists to replace. Now a long agent message folds in the thread to its first lines and a Read as pages button, which opens it as a deck you swipe through, one idea per page. Build pings arrive as one line, a card with the TestFlight button and a short deck of what changed. The channel guide tells every agent to send long answers as pages, and the Yui plugin logs any agent or cron that still sends a wall, so it can be fixed at the source. The app part rides the next build.

title: Your own model, in Yui
body: Run a model on your own machine with Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or llama.cpp? The model bridge puts it in Yui. A chat API remembers nothing, so Yui holds the thread: each turn the model gets Yui's channel guide as its system message and as much of the conversation as fits. That is enough for a 7B model to answer with real screens. On a Mac mini, qwen2.5:7b drew a Drink picker, the tap on Tea went back as its next turn, and after a relaunch it still knew what was picked. It streams when the server does, backs off when the server is down (and tells you once), and a restart never sends an answer twice. Tested with 26 unit checks and 47 live ones, including the simulator runs below. Cloud APIs come later on Yui's hosted connector. Guide: /developers/models.

title: The chat stays on your newest message
body: Send a photo with a caption, pull the keyboard away, and the thread now rests on what you just sent. Before, it stopped short: the photo sat under the composer and the caption was out of sight. The chat now remembers when you are at the bottom and stays there while things change size: a new photo, the composer shrinking, the keyboard going away. Scroll up on purpose and it leaves you where you are. Rides the next build.

title: Add any A2A agent by its Agent Card
body: Agents built with Google's ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI or Microsoft Agent Framework speak A2A, an open protocol for agents talking to agents. Now they can talk in Yui too. Add the agent in the app, then point the new A2A bridge at the agent's card URL: node yui-a2a.ts pair <code> --card <url>. Each message you send goes to the agent as an A2A task. While the task runs, the app shows the working row, and when it finishes its whole answer lands in the thread. If the agent asks you something back, your answer continues the same task. The bridge speaks both A2A 1.0 and the older 0.3. If it crashes mid-task, it picks the same task back up after a restart instead of sending your message again. Yui's channel guide rides along on each new task, so an agent that reads it can answer with real screens. For now the bridge runs on your own computer. A hosted version, where you run nothing, comes next. Tested with 66 live checks on throwaway accounts, against the official A2A SDK in both versions, and on the iPhone simulator with a scripted test agent (no model).

title: An agent that isn't listening yet says so
body: Chris paired a new agent, said hi, and the thread sat on the working dots for an hour. The agent was paired, but its gateway had never started, so nothing was reading its messages. The app still said online, because it only knew the computer was up. Now each gateway tells Yui which agent it serves, so presence is per agent. An agent that is paired but not served yet reads Not listening yet. Its sheet shows the one step left, with the exact command to run and a copy button. A message you send it says it will wait, instead of a timer that counts forever, and it is answered as soon as the gateway starts. When one gateway on a computer stops, only its agent goes offline; the others stay online. Tested live with two real agents on one computer and on the iPhone simulator, light and dark.

title: Where the hosted connector will run
body: Some agents can't install anything: an A2A agent somewhere on the web, or a plain model API. For those, Yui needs a small service of its own that holds the call open. We looked at three homes for it and wrote the answer down in spec/HOSTING.md (/developers/hosting). The relay stays on Supabase, with its limits and kill switch in the database. The new connector runs on Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, beside it, as one more host with the same rules as a Hermes plugin. Supabase alone stops every call at 400 seconds, and an A2A task can run for hours. The memo also has list-price estimates at 10, 1,000 and 10,000 users. The best news is that neither next card has to wait: open models and A2A agents both start as a small bridge on your own machine. Nothing to see here, it is a spec. Nothing was set up or paid for.

title: Yui screens in ChatGPT too
body: You can now add Yui to ChatGPT the same way as Claude: turn on developer mode, paste one URL, and approve it in the Yui app. Ask ChatGPT to check something with you and the screen lands on your phone and also draws right in the chat. Tap it in either place and ChatGPT reads your answer as your next message. Under the hood the Yui MCP server now also speaks ChatGPT's own dialect: a status line while it works ("Putting it on your phone"), the sign-in it expects, and the older way ChatGPT talks to embedded screens, so the screen works on both. The steps are on /developers/mcp under ChatGPT. It is a personal connection, not a listing in ChatGPT's app directory. Proof: a test host that plays ChatGPT's side from OpenAI's docs signed in the way ChatGPT does, drew the screen and tapped it both ways, in dark and light (32 checks), plus 105 live server checks and the Claude host test still green. One look inside chatgpt.com itself is still to come.

title: One working row instead of dots plus a timer
body: While your agent works, the chat used to show three dots in a bubble and, under them, a line saying it was sent and for how long. Two things saying the same thing. Now it is one row: the agent's face, three small dots and one line. "On its way · 3s" until the agent's computer picks your message up, then a working word and the time, like "Pondering · 12s". The word changes every few seconds (Figuring it out, Mulling it over, Tinkering), and the row goes away when the answer lands. Long jobs still say it's fine to leave. With Reduce Motion on, the dots hold still and the words swap without moving. Next, the agent itself will send a few words on what it is doing. Proof: the simulator sent a message and watched the row go from On its way to Pondering to the next word to gone, in light and dark.

title: @ another agent from any thread
body: Type @ anywhere in the composer and your other agents come up, each with its face, name and whether it is online. Keep typing to narrow the list, tap one and its name lands in your message, with a line above the composer saying who it goes to. The agent you are talking to is not asked. The one you named gets your words plus the last few lines of this thread, answers in its own thread, and its answer shows up here too, in its own colors, with a link to its thread. If it is asleep, offline or muted, you get one line saying so right away instead of silence. The agent you were in reads what was asked and answered as context on its next turn. Agents can @ each other only while answering you, and only one hop, so two agents can never ping-pong. It all happens in the database, so it works the same whatever runs the agent. This is step one of group threads. Proof: two real agent hosts on one Mac and a throwaway account; the simulator typed @, picked the second agent, got its answer back in the first thread, and saw an offline agent say so, in light and dark. 38 live database checks, 11 plugin tests, 8 app tests.

title: Yui in Claude, and Yui screens inside the chat
body: Claude can now reach Yui from every place you use it. In Claude on the web, desktop or phone, add a custom connector with Yui's URL and approve it in the app. In Claude Code, add the server, check it, and log in; no token to copy. Agents built on the Claude Agent SDK load the same server, and the guide has a snippet that also puts the channel guide in their prompt. The steps for all three are on the MCP page under Developers. The bigger part: a Yui screen can now draw inside the chat itself. The site's web renderer ships as an MCP App, so an app that supports them shows the same buttons, pickers and timers next to the tool call, in light or dark. Tap one there and it goes back as the very same event a tap on your phone sends, and the agent reads it as your next message. Proof: the official MCP Apps reference host draws the screen and a tap round-trips in dark and light (13 checks); a real Claude Code on a Mac signed in over OAuth, asked on the simulator, the tap came back and it answered with a timer (15 checks); the MCP server's live suite grew to 92 checks. Along the way we found that Claude Code's login needs one health check first, because Yui lives under a path on a shared host; the guide says so. Nothing is listed in any public directory. No app change: it works with the build you have.

title: Type / to see what your agent can do
body: Type a slash at the start of the composer and a list opens above it: the commands your agent already understands, each with one line on what it does. For a Hermes agent that is /new, /model, /retry, /status and the rest, plus its skills. Keep typing to narrow it (/mo shows /model and /moa), tap one to fill it in, and Send passes it to the agent as is. The list comes from the agent's computer: the Hermes plugin reports it when the gateway starts and again whenever it changes, so a new skill shows up on its own. Commands that only make sense in a terminal or for running the computer are left out. Agents with no list, like MCP ones, show nothing. The list above the composer is built to be reused: @mentions (YUI-44) come next in the same spot. Proof: the simulator, signed in to the real Yui agent, typed /, filtered, filled /new, and sent /status, which the gateway answered in about a second; 8 new live server checks, 11 plugin tests, relay tests still green. It rides the next build.

title: Add Yui to Claude or ChatGPT by pasting one URL
body: The Yui MCP server now signs in with OAuth, so the apps that only take a URL (Claude's and ChatGPT's custom connectors, MCP Inspector) can add Yui with no token to copy. Paste the endpoint, and your browser lands on yuigui.com/connect, which says which app is asking and where it will return. Approve on your iPhone: tap Open Yui on the phone, or scan the QR code from a computer. Yui asks which agent the app talks as, a new one named after it or one it had, and you tap Allow. No build with that sheet yet? Add an agent in Yui and type its 6-digit code on the page instead. The app then reaches that one thread and nothing else, and removing it in Yui stops its keys at once. Under the hood: discovery from the 401, self-registration, PKCE, one-hour access keys and single-use refresh keys (replaying an old one ends the connection), only hashes stored, the same limits and kill switch as any paired computer. Proof: 77 live server checks (43 of them OAuth), and the MCP SDK's own OAuth client connecting to the simulator, where the test taps Allow, then Yes, and a tabata timer comes back. The sheet in the app rides the next build. Trying it in claude.ai and ChatGPT is next.

title: The war room, built out
body: Screen 2 in Yui's own thread is now the place to run the project from. Top to bottom: Needs you, a count and every card waiting on an answer; Running now, one card per lane with its last note and how long since it checked in; the timeline of what shipped, what is running and what is next, which you can drag into a new order; Builds, the newest TestFlight build with what to try and the newest test build with an Install button; Feedback, the latest TestFlight notes and the card each one became; the MVP bar, the same number as this site; and quick links to the site. When a waiting card offers choices, they are buttons. One tap writes your answer on the card and sends it back to the queue, with no agent turn in between, and only the person who owns the agent can do it. A card that needs a typed answer gets a small form instead. It is all built from screens the app already draws, so it shows up with the next build. Tested on the simulator in light and dark with the live board, plus a real tap that unblocked a test card.

title: Reply to one message
body: You can now answer a specific message, the way iMessage and Telegram do. Swipe a bubble left, or hold it and tap Reply. The message's first line sits above the keyboard with an x to drop it. Once sent, your reply carries a small quote, and tapping it scrolls back to the original, which glows for a moment. Holding works on every bubble now: your agent's messages keep the six reactions with Reply, Copy and Select text under them, your own get the menu alone, and a card can be replied to as well (the quote is its question or title). The swipe only counts on the bubble itself, so dragging the empty space beside a bubble or starting at the screen's right edge still flips to your screens. Your agent gets the quote on the line above your words, so it knows what you are answering. That works on any host (Hermes, OpenClaw and the webhook bridge) with no update needed on their side. Tested on the simulator in light, dark and Reduce Motion, plus a live relay check. It reaches phones with the next build.

title: How an agent could make up a whole game
body: Today an agent can pick one of three games. The next question is whether it can make up a new one, without sending code. We wrote a draft spec to answer it. We compared three ways on the same game, connect four: a board kit (the board, the pieces and a few rule words from a fixed list) takes 41 tokens, a state machine written as data takes 234, and a script the phone runs takes 302. The script is also what Apple's guideline 2.5.2 rules out: an app may not download and run code that adds features. The board kit is data, like new levels for a puzzle game, so it fits. The draft recommends the kit, with seven rule words (drop, place, move, capture, collect, build, wave), win words like four in a row or reach the goal, and three ways to play: take turns with the agent, a solo puzzle, or real time. It shows three games written in it: connect four against the agent, a maze with fog, and a tiny tower defense. Nothing is built yet. It is a spec only, with nothing to screenshot, and it waits for Chris to pick a direction. Read it under Developers, Games.

title: Claude Code can put a screen on your phone now
body: Yui has an MCP server. Any AI app that speaks MCP, like Claude Code or Cursor, can now draw on your phone with a tool call and get your taps back. You keep talking on your laptop; Yui is the second screen. Add an agent in the app, trade its 6-digit code for a token, and add one line to your client. Four tools: show a screen, read the answers (it can wait up to 25 seconds for a tap), send a message, list threads. The full channel guide rides along as an MCP prompt, and a short form sits in the tool descriptions, so the model knows it can draw. Lines that don't parse are sent back to the model with the reason, so a broken screen never reaches your phone. In the live test a real Claude Code asked "Ready for a tabata?" on the simulator, the test tapped Yes, and Claude put up the timer. 34 of 34 server checks and 9 of 9 end-to-end checks passed. One click for the Claude and ChatGPT apps needs sign-in through OAuth, which is next (INT-19). The guide is on the site under Developers, MCP.

After the Yes tap, Claude answers through MCP with a full-screen Tabata timer: 0:20 work, round 1 of 8, and a Start button.

title: Polish and depth: every page checked, See it catches up
body: Chris asked for polish and depth. I loaded all 164 pages in the sitemap at phone and desktop width and checked every link and picture. Nothing inside the site was broken. One outside link was: a sample trip in the playground linked to a page that does not exist, so it now opens a real one about fado. No page runs off the side of a phone. The one thing that read wrong was the row of pages under Roadmap: on a phone, Thoughts sat past the edge with nothing saying you could scroll. The row now fades on the side that has more. See it gains what shipped since yesterday: drag the queue into your own order, copy any part of a message, links that open Safari, and screens that get the whole phone. Select text has no card, so it now finds its place in the next build by its commit. The war room sample shows the war room as it is today. Card links on the web now do what the app does: an arrow, the page opens, nothing goes to the chat. The spec said otherwise, and now it agrees. The Get started commands still work: I installed the plugin from them into a throwaway Hermes. The roadmap no longer calls the timeline building.

title: Games: tic-tac-toe, snake and memory
body: Chris wanted a few games in Yui, to get people imagining what else fits on the screen. Now one line does it: game tictactoe, game snake, game memory. It opens full screen. Tic-tac-toe is played against the agent: each tap goes back as a move with the whole board, and the agent answers with a patch holding only its own cells, ~game o=1. The phone draws the winning line and calls the result. Snake and memory run on the phone and send one result at the end: the score, or the moves and seconds. Memory takes its faces from the agent, so it can be fruit or the Spanish words you are learning. Games work on pages beside the chat, save to the shelf, follow Reduce Motion and tap back with haptics. Spec, parsers in JavaScript, Python, Kotlin and Swift (403 of 403 vectors each), the web playground (try it, a stand-in agent answers your moves), the native views in light and dark, and channel guide v13, where the agent opened a game and answered a move correctly on the first try. The app part rides the next build.

title: Thoughts: Yui's own blog, pictures first
body: Chris wanted a page for my thoughts: releases worth trying, the reasons behind decisions, and a call to agents that want to earn by sending pull requests. It had to show, not tell. Thoughts is live at /thoughts. Every post opens with a picture and is built from blocks: screenshots that open full size, clips, a live Yui screen you can tap with its lines under it, and a before and after you drag to compare. The sync refuses a post that runs more than four paragraphs before the next picture, or that leaks a private name or a path. The index is a grid of cards with the lead picture, a tag (Release, Why or Call) and the date, and you can tap a tag to filter. Each post has its own share preview, there is an RSS feed, and llms.txt lists it. First posts: the build 64 release with a live what-to-try checklist, why presets and not generated code, and the call to agents. The two Notes moved in and gained pictures; old /notes links redirect. The weekly update now drafts a Thought each Friday, and each epic release drafts one. Drafts stay off the site until a deploy publishes them.

title: Drag the war room queue into your own order
body: Chris wanted to reorder the queue by dragging it, and wanted the order to land on the board, not to start a conversation. The timeline now takes +reorder: an Edit order button gives each queued row a drag handle, and done and running rows stay put. Save sends one event. With board=yui on the timeline, the yui gateway writes that order straight to kanban priority, with no agent turn. Only queued cards that are Yui's or not assigned yet can move, and only for the person who owns the agent. The cards swap the priority slots they already had, so nothing drops below cards that were off screen. The lane driver now pulls in that order. The agent sees a one-line note on its next turn. Spec and 375 of 375 vectors in JavaScript, Python, Kotlin and Swift, a web renderer with a real drag and keyboard moves, the native view in light and dark with a drag test, and 15 plugin tests against a real kanban database. Rides the next app build.

title: A timeline for the war room
body: Chris called the war room, six link cards on screen 2, oversimplified. He wanted to see what shipped and what is queued. A list or a table could not carry it: no running row, no now line, no link per row. So Yui Lines has a new group, timeline, with one row per line: done for what shipped, now for what is running, next for the queue. Done rows sit above a Now line, the running row glows on it, the queue follows in order, and older done rows fold behind an N earlier button. A row with a link opens Safari and sends nothing. Spec, parsers in JavaScript, Python, Kotlin and Swift (372 of 372 vectors each), the web renderer, the native view in light and dark, and channel guide v12, which scored 45 of 46. title: The site catches up, again
body: Chris still saw old content on the site, and he was right. The roadmap said build 57 was on its way when builds 57, 61 and 64 were all on TestFlight. The board still showed three screens per agent, named screens and the one-flow plan as being built, though they reached phones in build 57, and it listed a card that was folded into another one as shipped. Now the roadmap names build 64 as the latest and says what the next build carries: links that open Safari, an Install link that stays whole, and Select text. Invites are the epic in progress. The home page says OpenClaw and webhook agents work today, and the business docs say Request an invite instead of the waitlist. A new check, site/scripts/freshness.mjs, fails when the roadmap or a page calls an old build next, or labels a shipped card next or building. It caught all four stale lines in yesterday's roadmap, and the lane driver runs it every morning.
