title: Build to earn, the proposal
body: Chris wants a crypto lawyer to read /earn, so the page is now a real proposal. It opens with our position: ownership in Yui is earned by work, not bought. No money changes hands, so we think a stake earned here should not be treated like a sale of securities, and we would rather make that case in the open. Then four forms it could take, as options and not decisions: points with equity on its own path, options or restricted units for work, profits interests in an LLC, and a community round later that stays apart from earning. Then ten numbered questions for counsel, one card each, so a lawyer can answer inline: Howey and work as an investment, Rule 701, who owns what an agent earns, holders of record, tradable versus restricted, the 2026 US posture, tax, how to test our position, who votes the community pool, and whether the page itself is an offer. Answers get posted under each question. Nothing mints before that, and not before Chris signs off. The draft banner stays: no token exists, and nothing is for sale.

images.alt: Our position on /earn in light mode, with Chris's line about the Supreme Court and the first two forms it could take

title: Copy any part of a message
body: Chris wanted to copy just a piece of what his agent said, not the whole message. Now when you hold an agent's message, the menu has Select text under Copy. It opens the words on their own page, where you can read them but not type. Drag to pick the part you want and tap Copy, or tap Copy all. When the message sits at the bottom of the screen, it now moves up so the menu never covers it. Replying to one message, the way iMessage does, is next on the list as YUI-68. On main now, it goes out with the next TestFlight build.

title: Links in a card open Safari
body: Chris tapped Install on a card that was meant to open a web page. Instead the app sent the word Install back to the agent, and the agent answered with the same card again. Now a card with a link gets a small arrow on its button. Tapping it opens the page in Safari and sends nothing to the chat, so the agent never answers a tap that already did its job. Buttons without a link still answer the agent as before. We also checked that long install links survive whole: over 300 characters, with a fragment, encoded parts, & and =, even when they arrive one character at a time. On main now, it rides the next TestFlight build. The picture is the web playground drawing the same card; the build entry will carry the phone.

title: Build 64: hold to talk, with a waveform and a trash can
body: Chris held the mic and the app closed again. The crash log said build 57, the build from before the fix, so the phone had not picked up build 61 yet. To be sure, we ran the old code on a simulator with the mic and speech allowed, the way a phone has them, and it crashed in the same spot. The fixed code does not. While in there, hold to talk got the feel Chris asked for, like WhatsApp: while you hold, a waveform moves with your voice next to a clock. Let go and your words send. Slide left to the trash can and let go, and nothing sends. With Reduce Motion on, the waveform is one still bar that fills as you speak. After a voice send the keyboard stays down.

title: Demo clips of every preset, recorded from the app
short: Short clips show each preset working on a real phone: a timer, a choice, a chart, a gallery and more.
body: Each Yui preset now has a short clip recorded in the iPhone simulator, one tall for phones and one wide for pages. They come from a script, so a new preset gets its clip the same way and the clips stay true to the app. The clips are on the home page and in posts.

title: A drafter writes Yui's social posts, and a person signs off
body: Yui's posts need to sound like Yui. A daily job now drafts them from what shipped, and a copy checker holds each draft to the same plain-words rules as this site: no hype words, no dashes, no private names. Nothing is posted by itself. Every draft waits in a queue for a person to read and approve it. There is nothing to see on a phone, so this entry has no picture. The code is public.

title: Build to earn, a first draft
body: Chris asked for a V1 of build to earn on the site, so there is something to look at. It lives at /earn and says draft at the top: no token exists yet, and nothing is for sale. The idea is plain. Yui is built by whoever shows up, human or agent, and only work earns: a merged pull request, or TestFlight feedback that ships. Two doors, one for people and one for agents, with a short note written to agents. Points on a public ledger come first, tokens only after a legal review. Badges like First Contributor and Hat Trick are shown as planned. The contribute page, the footer and llms.txt now point to it.

title: Screens get the whole phone
body: Chris looked at a plan on screen 2 on build 57 and said the screens should be full screen. Now they are: off the chat, the top bar with your agents and settings goes away, and so does the composer. title: As many screens as the agent needs, up to 12
body: Chris sent a screen to screen 2 on build 57 and asked for more. Now an agent can use screens 2 through 12, and a screen only exists once something is on it: send to screen 5 alone and you get the chat plus one page. Clearing a screen takes it away. The switcher above the composer is now a small chat icon and one dot per screen, and with only the chat it is gone. Screen 13 and up stay in the chat. The rule changed in the spec and all four parsers, with new test vectors, and the agent guide now says screens 2 to 12. It rides the next build.

title: Build 61: holding the mic no longer crashes
body: A tester held the talk button on build 57 and the app closed. The crash log showed why: the speech permission answer, the mic and the live transcript all arrive on system threads, and the code that took them expected the main one, so Swift stopped the app on the spot. They now hand off to the main thread properly, and a mic with no usable input (a call, a route change) says it can't listen instead of crashing. A new test crashed on the old code and passes now. Shipped alone as a hotfix in build 61.

title: Build 57: every fix you sent is on your phone
body: This morning's TestFlight notes were all fixed in the code by lunch, but none of them reached a phone: Apple's daily upload limit held every build after 33. Build 57 went live tonight, so we checked each note again on that exact code. The message box empties after you send, on every path. The X and Done on a photo gallery close it. Photos keep to their own space, including tall phone screenshots, which were the ones still overlapping in the last note; a new test sends four of them in every gallery layout and checks nothing runs under the card below. A long answer shows the agent is working and for how long, instead of telling you to restart. Narration skips the robot voices. There are more colors to pick from. And you can send a photo, or hold the mic to talk.

title: Request an invite: the waitlist is now the way into the beta
body: The waitlist on yuigui.com is gone. In its place, at the bottom of every page, is Request an invite: first name, last name, email and phone. The email field says to use the one on your Apple ID, because that is where TestFlight sends the invite. Under the form, three steps say what happens next: we review your request, Apple emails you a TestFlight invite, you open it on your iPhone, install Yui and sign in with Apple. A request lands in the invites table as requested, written by the site's server, never by the browser. Asking twice with the same email just says thank you again. The public TestFlight link stays for people who already run Hermes. Bots get a hidden field and a rate limit, UTM tags still say which post brought someone, and the privacy page has a link right under the form. Next: agents that come with an invite (YUI-57).

images.alt: The Request an invite form on a phone: first name, last name, email with the hint to use the email on your Apple ID, phone, three next steps and a Request an invite button
The Request an invite form on a desktop page, below the TestFlight, GitHub and Lend your agent cards

title: Invites: ask, get approved, Apple emails you, sign in and you're in
body: Yui's beta now has an invite path next to the public TestFlight link. A request (name, the email on your Apple ID, phone) lands in a new server-only table, and nothing goes out until Chris approves it. Approving adds you as a tester to a TestFlight group through Apple's API, so the invite email comes from Apple and Yui sends none of its own. When you first sign in with Apple, the app matches your invite by that email. If you hide your email, the invite link yuigui.com/i/<code> opens the app with the code, or you type it under Invite code on the sign-in screen. Codes work once, are stored only as a hash, and wrong guesses are rate limited. Deleting your account deletes your invite. The privacy page lists the new fields. Next: the request form on the site (SITE-26) and agents that come with an invite (YUI-57).

images.alt: Yui's sign-in screen with an invite waiting: Invite ABCDE-FGHJK is ready. Sign in to join.
A note at the top of Yui: That invite code didn't work. It may be used already. Ask for a new link.

title: Test builds by link: new app builds on the phone without TestFlight
body: Apple lets an app upload only so many TestFlight builds a day, and Yui hit that limit today. So main now has a second way onto the phone. scripts/devbuild.sh builds the app straight from main as an ad hoc build, keeps it in a private storage bucket behind links that expire in 7 days, and sends a card with an Install button into the Yui thread. Tap it and iOS installs the new build over the old one, sign-in and threads included. Ad hoc builds install only on iPhones registered to the developer account, so a forwarded link does nothing anywhere else. It runs when asked, and on its own when new app work lands on main, at most once every few hours. Along the way the card component learned url=: its button can now open a web page or an install link as well as answering the agent. This one is a script and a button, so no screenshots.

title: The site catches up: what is on your phone, and what comes with build 57
body: Before going back to the app, the site had to match the app. Cards that are done in the code but not on TestFlight yet now say so: on the Shipped log, on See it and on the board they read Next build, with a line that they reach TestFlight with the next build. Those labels come from the Builds page's data, so they turn into Shipped on their own the day build 57 goes live. The roadmap names build 57 and the eight cards it carries, drops the lock screen timer from the parked list (it is in that build), and lists accounts and the relay as one line. The sign-up form at the bottom of each page now says join for updates, since the beta is open to anyone. And a push to GitHub deploys the site again: the hosting project was pointed at the wrong folder.

title: Yui@home: lend your idle agent to Yui
body: Like SETI@home, but for AI tokens. If your Claude or ChatGPT Codex plan has tokens left over, your agent can pick a card off the Yui backlog and open a pull request that a person reviews. Today this ships the story and the signposts: the note Donate your idle tokens to Yui, a Contribute with your agent page under Developers with a prompt to try now and a feature spec template (docs/specs in the hub repo), a Lend your agent option at the bottom of every page and on Get started, a For AI agents section on Developers, and llms.txt at the site root so an assistant researching Yui can pass the invitation on. The agent-ready backlog export and weekly routine prompts per platform are OSS-6, after the MVP.

body: Apple approved Yui for public beta testing. Anyone with an iPhone can install it from TestFlight at https://testflight.apple.com/join/ykrYHwet, no invite needed, up to 10,000 testers. title: Three short videos: Yui in 15 seconds, Yui Lines in 30, your Hermes on your phone in 60
body: Three videos you can watch with the sound off, each in 9:16 for phones and 16:9 for everything else. Yui in 15 seconds: you ask, a screen answers, three times over: a Tabata timer, a question with buttons, a chart. Yui Lines in 30 seconds: one line of text typed out, then the timer it draws, running, then the honest token count from the benchmark: 1.6x fewer tokens than minified JSON, 2.7x fewer than pretty JSON, 3.9x fewer than a component tree, across the same ten screens. Your Hermes on your phone in 60 seconds: add an agent in the app, get a code, install the plugin, pair, restart the gateway, and the agent says hi with its first screen. The commands are the same ones on yuigui.com/start. Everything is recorded in the iPhone simulator on the demo account, so the pairing code is the placeholder 123456 and the agent's words are scripted; in the app it is your own Hermes and your own model talking. They live on See it under Videos, with a press kit at the bottom of that page (both cuts, posters and the wordmark to download), and each has a share link. Social posts are drafts for now: nothing goes out until Chris says so.

body: Every screen on See it, every playground sample and every recorded clip now has its own short link, like yuigui.com/s/timer. Paste one into a chat or a post and the preview card shows the Yui Lines on the left and the real screen they draw on the right, captured from the same renderer you can tap on the page. title: Draw your best screen in three lines: a community page and the first open challenge
body: Yui Lines is open, and now there is a front door for people who want to build with it. The new Community page, under Developers, says who builds with Yui Lines today (honestly: us, plus the Hermes, OpenClaw and webhook adapters), and lists six ways to join in: a parser (Rust is next), a preset idea, a renderer, an adapter, a conformance vector, or the app itself. It also opens the first challenge: draw your best screen in three lines or fewer. You add your lines to one file in the repo and open a pull request. A small checker runs on every pull request: it parses each entry with the reference parser and says ok, or exactly what to fix, like a misspelled preset or a fourth line. Merged entries show up in a gallery on the page, drawn live in your browser, each with an Open in the playground link that loads its lines ready to edit. We seeded it with five of our own. Both CONTRIBUTING guides now point there.

images.alt: The gallery on the community page in dark mode: three live phones showing a morning check-in with a sleep slider, a Tabata timer, and a weekly weigh-in with a stat and a line chart, each with its Yui Lines below and an Open in the playground link.
The community page on a phone in light mode: the heading Build with Yui Lines, and the open challenge, draw your best screen in 3 lines.
Two card grids: who builds with Yui Lines (the app, the Hermes plugin, the OpenClaw plugin, the webhook bridge, this website) and six ways to contribute, each with a link.

title: The go-to-market plan is public
body: How Yui finds its people now lives on one page: yuigui.com/business/gtm. It folds the content plan and the social accounts plan into a single current plan. Who it is for, in order: Hermes users, then OpenClaw users, then other agent builders and people who like specs. What we say and never say, with the token numbers always given as the split (1.6x fewer than minified JSON, 3.9x fewer than a component tree). Five content pillars, a plan for each channel with its gate, a weekly rhythm, and the first 30 days, starting Monday Sep 28. It also says what grassroots means for us: an open screen language anyone can parse and render, real ways to contribute at every size, show-and-tell with credit, and a monthly Yui Lines challenge. Nothing has been posted and no account has been created. Every post and every community message waits for Chris, and the plan ends with his five open questions. There is a matching Google Doc, linked from the page.

images.alt: The go-to-market page on yuigui.com: the weekly rhythm table, then the first 30 days, days 1 to 7.
The top of the go-to-market plan on a phone: the title, the Google Doc link and the links to the older content and social plans.

title: OpenClaw agents can talk in Yui now
body: Yui worked with Hermes agents and with anything that answers a web request. Now it works with OpenClaw too, the way it works with Hermes: as a channel, right inside OpenClaw. You install the Yui plugin, type the code the app shows, restart OpenClaw, and your agent answers on your phone. It keeps its own memory, tools and sessions; Yui is just one more place it can talk, like Telegram or Slack. Every turn, the plugin gives the agent the Yui channel guide, with one plain line on top: on Yui, draw screens in Yui Lines, not A2UI, the widget format OpenClaw's own app uses. So the agent answers hi with buttons, and gets the tap back. It keeps the same delivery promise as the Hermes plugin: every message reaches the agent once, in order, and every answer lands once, even if OpenClaw is killed mid-thought. Cron jobs can send to Yui too. A live test runs a real OpenClaw in a throwaway setup, on a throwaway account, with a stand-in model that records exactly what OpenClaw told it: the guide was there, the screen came back, the tap reached the agent, a kill in the middle of a turn was replayed once, a message answered but not receipted was not answered twice, a clean stop showed offline, and messages sent while it was down went in as one turn. 24 of 24 checks passed. A developer tool, so nothing new on the phone. The guide is on the site under Developers, OpenClaw.

images.alt: The OpenClaw page on yuigui.com: install the Yui channel plugin, pair with the app's code, turn the channel on and restart the gateway.
The Developers page on yuigui.com with a new OpenClaw card next to Connect your agent and the Webhook bridge.

title: Three screens per agent: the chat, then screens 2 and 3 a swipe away
body: Every agent in Yui now has three screens side by side. The chat is the first. Screens 2 and 3 sit to its right, a swipe away, with small Chat, 2, 3 tabs above the composer. An agent sends there what should stay put while you keep talking: a focus timer on 2, your shopping list on 3. A page keeps what lands on it across replies until the agent clears it. When a reply sends something there, the page slides over with a spring, or cross-fades if Reduce Motion is on, and the chat keeps a small On screen 3 pill that takes you back. A line sent to a page beats the full-screen defaults, so a focus timer stays on its page; a workout still takes the whole phone. The Yui Lines spec has a new Pages rule and a pageOf function, and all four parsers pass 349 of 349 test cases. The channel guide (v11) tells agents when to use a page. It scored 44 of 45 on Opus 5.5, and the new case (keep a list in sight while planning a recipe) put the list on screen 3.

title: Polish: Developers and the playground
body: A polish pass on /developers, the spec pages and /playground. Every spec is now one tap from /developers. On a phone the sample picker sits above the phone, and while you type the phone pins to the top so the keyboard never hides what you are drawing. Every button, tab and link on these pages is at least 44 points tall on a phone, the footer and spec index included. The playground samples use generic agent names. Lighthouse accessibility is 100 on both pages, no page scrolls sideways at 390 or 1280 in light or dark, and all 56 samples render with no console errors.

The playground on a phone: the sample picker and Stream button above the phone, with 44 point tall tabs.
The Every spec row on the Developers page: Yui Lines, Channel guide, Reactions, Benchmark, Agents, Relay, Adapters and Preset flywheel.

title: Not on Hermes? Any agent that answers a web request can talk in Yui now
body: Until today, an agent needed Hermes to reach Yui. Now there is a webhook bridge, in Python and in Node, with nothing to install beyond the language itself. You run it next to your agent: it pairs with the same code the app shows, dials out to Yui so your machine opens no ports, and sends each turn to your agent as one web request. Your agent answers with text, or with a screen in Yui Lines, and the bridge writes it into the thread. Every request carries the channel guide, so the agent knows it can draw. It keeps the same delivery promise as the Hermes plugin: every message reaches the agent once, in order, and every answer lands once, even if the bridge is killed mid-thought or the network drops. Each language comes with a ten-line example agent that answers hi with three buttons and replies to the tap. A live test runs both bridges on a throwaway account: a screen round trip, a tap, a kill in the middle of a turn, a crash between the answer and its receipt, a clean stop, messages sent while it was down. 44 of 44 checks passed. A developer tool, so nothing new on the phone. The guide is on the site under Developers, Webhook bridge.

images.alt: The Webhook bridge page on yuigui.com: what the bridge does, the Python and Node clients with their ten-line example agents, and the five-minute setup.
The Developers page on yuigui.com with a new Webhook bridge card: not on Hermes, any agent that answers an HTTP POST can talk in Yui.

title: The preset flywheel: custom screens that keep coming back become presets
body: Presets cover what agents usually show. For the rest there is custom, a small JSON escape hatch. Now the Yui plugin for Hermes can note which custom screens an agent sends, by shape only: a boarding pass becomes ticket{flight:s,gate:s,seat:s}, never the seat or the flight. No text, number, link or id from a screen is ever written, and tests push every conformance vector and 400 random screens full of marked values through it to prove it. It is off unless the agent's owner turns it on, and the log never leaves their machine. A weekly report ranks the shapes by how many different days they came back, and when one clears the bar (5 uses on 3 days) the owner gets one message in Yui. The checklist for promoting a shape, from the spec line to all four parsers, the playground, the native iPhone view and the channel guide, is a new spec page. Nothing to see in the app itself: this one is plumbing.

title: Save a screen, bring it back with two tokens: every agent gets a shelf
body: An agent can now keep a screen for later. save busy day puts the screen it just drew on a shelf at the top of the thread. Tap a chip on the shelf and it opens full screen, fresh, with no message sent and no tokens spent. In a later reply the agent brings it back with show busy day, and forget busy day takes it off. A screen saved on the full-screen stage opens there again, and taps on a screen that came back tell the agent which one it was. Hold a chip to remove it yourself. The shelf rebuilds from the thread, so it follows you to a new phone. Measured on the 10 benchmark screens: bringing a screen back costs 21 tokens in total against 338 to send them again as Yui Lines and 530 as minified JSON, 16x less. show workout is 2 tokens. The Yui Lines spec, all four parsers (347 of 347 test cases each), the playground and the app all do it. The channel guide (v10) tells agents to save what people will reuse. The eval scores it 42 of 44 on Opus 5.5, and both new saved-screen cases pass.

images.alt: A chat with Yui in dark mode. Two chips at the top, check-in and busy day, are saved screens. Further down, the agent answered 'Pull up my busy day workout' with the Tabata timer.
The busy day Tabata reopened full screen from the shelf in light mode: 0:20 work, round 1 of 8, and a Start button.

title: A polish pass on See it, Get started and Timeline
body: A look at three pages on a phone and a laptop, light and dark. No page scrolls sideways at 390 pixels and all 539 links and pictures on them load. Get started now says it up front: in the beta Yui has no agent of its own, you bring your own Hermes, with the install command right there to copy. On a phone, the row of pages under Roadmap and Developers now scrolls so the page you are on is never cut off at the edge. See it gained two entries: a plan that ends in Send (YUI-53) and the Timeline page (SITE-16), and site pages now say On yuigui.com instead of claiming the app. Its live phones start drawing a screen earlier, so a quick scroll does not catch them blank. One older screenshot showed a private agent name in a notification; the name is now blurred.

title: Read, answer, send once: a plan is now one full-screen flow
body: Chris got three thin pages of findings, had to close them, and then answered two questions somewhere else. Now it is one flow. A plan can hold pages to read before its questions, it opens full screen, and one button at the end sends every answer. When it closes, the chat keeps a record: a small card with the plan's title and what it held (2 pages, 2 answers) that opens to the pages, and the answers as your own message, as if you had typed them. The agent still gets one event with everything. The Yui Lines spec, all four parsers (335 of 335 test cases each), the playground and the app all do it. The channel guide (v9) tells agents that findings then questions is one plan and that a page needs a real paragraph. The old guide failed both new test cases the same way Chris saw it live; v9 scored 42 of 42.

images.alt: A plan open full screen in Yui: step 1 of 4, a page titled What broke with a paragraph and two bullet points, and Back and Next buttons.

title: Scroll up, and one arrow brings you back
body: Long threads now have a way home. Scroll up more than about a screen and a round down arrow shows just above the composer. If your agent answers while you're up there, the arrow counts the new messages. One tap and you're back at the newest one, and the arrow goes away. Scroll down by hand and it goes too, and sending a message from up the thread takes you straight to it. We also checked the composer empties in every way you can send: typing, a photo with a caption, a tap on a screen, a reaction, and a message queued while offline, each with its own test. With Reduce Motion on, a sent message fades in instead of floating up.

images.alt: A long chat scrolled up, light mode. A round down arrow sits above the composer with a red 3 on its corner for three new messages.
The same arrow with its count of 3 in dark mode.
After the tap: the thread at its newest message, the three new notes from the agent in view, and no arrow.
Eight frames 40 milliseconds apart: a sent message starts small at the composer and floats up into its place in the thread.

title: Watch Yui grow: the whole history on one page
body: Yui is built in public, so every step is already on GitHub. The new Timeline page, under Roadmap, reads it back. Press play and it steps through every shipped change that has a screenshot, oldest first, while four counters climb: app commits, site commits, TestFlight builds and changes shipped. Drag the slider to jump to any moment. Below it, each day lists what shipped and each build, by the minute, with its screenshots, and every commit that day links to GitHub. It rebuilds itself from the git history whenever the site deploys, and it checks every line against the same list that keeps private names off the public board.

images.alt: The Timeline page on a laptop: Watch Yui grow, with a Coach tabata timer screenshot on the left and counters on the right reading 19 app commits, 48 site commits, 16 builds and 35 shipped, above a play button and a slider at 16 of 39.

title: No dead buttons: a plan ends in Send, and agents stop adding 'Got it'
body: Chris spotted two things. The last button of a question flow said "Create project" even when nothing was a project. And agents sometimes ended a card with a lone "Got it" button that did nothing. Now a plan's last button says Send, in the app, on the site and in all three Yui Lines parsers. The channel guide every agent gets (v8) says every button does something: no buttons that only acknowledge, a card with nothing to act on has no button, and a submit is named for what happens. The channel eval now fails any reply with a dead button and has three new cases that tempt one. It scored 38 of 40, and neither miss was a button.

images.alt: The review step of a plan in Yui: the last answer, Home and Contact, with one purple Send button under it.

title: Yui Lines back on the front page, and every spec on the site
body: The home page now says how Yui works: one line of Yui Lines next to the timer it draws, live, with the honest benchmark (1.6x fewer tokens than minified JSON, 3.9x fewer than a component tree). /yl opens with a quick start: five lines, five screens, tap one to draw it, copy one into your agent. And every spec in the repo now reads on the site under Developers > Specs: agents, the relay, adapters and the benchmark join Yui Lines, the channel guide and reactions, each with an index on the left and a link to every section. The pages are built from the repo files on every deploy, and the build stops if a spec names someone it should not.

images.alt: The home page How it works band: the line timer 40/20x8 Tabata beside a live phone drawing that Tabata timer, two stat boxes saying 1.6x fewer tokens than minified JSON and 3.9x fewer than a component tree, and buttons to the Yui Lines spec and the playground.
The Yui Lines page: a quick start listing five lines, each with a Copy button, a phone drawing the selected line, and the spec below with an index of every section on the left.

title: React to a message: hold it, tap 👍, and your agent builds it
body: Hold any message from your agent and a bar of six reactions floats above it, the way Telegram and iMessage do it. Each one is an instruction, not a mood: 👍 build it, 👎 no, 🤔 not sure (the agent asks a few short questions, one screen each), ❤️ love it (kept as a preference), ⏳ later (parked as a card or note), 🔥 priority. The reaction reaches the agent as one turn with the start of your message quoted, so it knows what you mean, and the emoji stays on the bubble when you come back. What each one means lives in one file, spec/REACTIONS.md, which also writes the Reactions section of the channel guide every agent gets; it is public at yuigui.com/reactions. The guide scored 37 of 37 in the channel eval, including three new reaction cases. End to end in the simulator: a real model got the 👍 and built the plan (a card, a checklist and timers) without asking again.

images.alt: Holding the agent's message: the thread dims, the message lifts and a bar of six reactions sits above it with a label under each, build it, no, not sure, love it, later, priority, and Copy below.
The message with a thumbs up badge on its corner after the tap.
Dark mode, after reopening: the thumbs up is still on the proposal, and under it the agent's answer, a Saturday session card, a checklist and a timer.

title: Yui Lines in Python and Kotlin
body: Yui Lines had two parsers: JavaScript for the site and Swift for the app. Now it has four. Python is one file with no dependencies, so an agent plugin, a webhook or a demo agent can read the same lines the app draws. Kotlin runs on the JVM and is the start of an Android parser. Both pass all 333 shared test vectors in 20 files, the same ones the JavaScript and Swift parsers pass, read straight from the spec folder with no copies. We also fed each one 20,000 random documents and compared every result with the JavaScript parser: no differences. One new script, spec/conformance/run-all.sh, runs every language and prints a pass count for each. The Developers page now lists all four parsers. Rust is next, and it is a good first contribution.

images.alt: The Developers page on yuigui.com: a new Parsers section lists four Yui Lines parsers, JavaScript, Swift, Python and Kotlin, each linked to its source, with a note that spec/conformance/run-all.sh runs them all and that Rust is next

title: The timer keeps counting on the lock screen
body: Start a timer an agent sent and lock the phone: it keeps going. The lock screen shows the timer's name, the round you are on, work or rest, the time left in this phase and in the whole workout, and a bar that fills as the phase runs. The Dynamic Island shows a ring and the clock, and opens to the same controls. Pause, resume or end the timer right there, no need to open the app. The rounds advance and the beeps keep sounding with the phone locked, and it wears the look of the agent that sent it. When the last round ends it says Done and leaves on its own. A timer set to silent has no sound to play, so on the lock screen it counts the current phase and catches up on the next round when you open Yui.

title: Notes: longer pieces, starting with why Yui is open source

body: The See it page used to hold three static mockups drawn by hand. Now it shows every screen Yui can draw today: 36 of them, from 25 shipped cards. Each preset is a live phone that draws the same Yui Lines an agent sends, so you can tap it, with the line printed beside it. Where the iPhone app has a recording or a screenshot, it sits next to the live one: nine demo clips, plus first run, change your answer and full screen. Every entry names the card that built it and the day it shipped, and the card id opens it on the board. The board links back with a See it button, and card ids on the roadmap now link to their screens. Four planned cards (voice, the onboarding interview, meal photo to macros, more screens per agent) get a mock drawn on the web and a clear label: not built. This also closes SITE-7, the preset gallery.

title: Who the first outside testers are
body: A plan for the first 20 to 50 people outside the project to try Yui: what a tester needs (an iPhone on iOS 26 and a Hermes that already works), cohorts of 1, 5, 20 and 50 with a gate before each, and 32 public places where Hermes and OpenClaw users gather, each with its size, its rules on self-promotion and what we would say there. The invites are drafts: nothing has been posted or sent, and each one waits for Chris. OpenClaw users are told the honest route for now, importing into Hermes, until the OpenClaw adapter exists. A plan with nothing to see, so no screenshots. Read it at yuigui.com/business/beta-list.

title: The playground reads right to a screen reader
body: The playground was the one page under 95 on Lighthouse accessibility. The screen picker, the YL text box and the stream speed slider now carry names a screen reader can announce, and the Start button on the Arnold timer uses dark ink on orange instead of white, which was too faint to pass contrast. Every page on the site now scores 95 or better.

Now the menu has five items: What it does, See it, Roadmap, Developers and Get Yui. Roadmap holds the live board, the ship log (this page) and the build list in one row of tabs. Developers is a new page that points at the playground, the Yui Lines spec and the channel guide. Phases are listed only on the roadmap now, so they cannot drift apart again.

title: Every color on one screen
body: Beta feedback: "I'm going to want a wider variety of colors." The Add agent picker was a sideways row that showed six warm looks and hid the rest past the edge, so it read as oranges and pinks only. It is now a grid with every look on screen, sorted around the hue wheel, and six new colors fill the gaps: cherry, honey, lime, teal, grape and slate. That makes 22 colors plus the six personality sets, all passing the AA contrast check in light and dark. Agents can pick the new ones too: theme teal.

title: Two common slips now parse
body: Agents writing Yui Lines make the same two mistakes. They write options as separate quoted strings, choose "Where?" "Camera roll" "Drafts", which used to come out as one long question with nothing to tap. And they patch with the add's own head, ~card@week, which never parsed. The parser now reads two or more trailing quoted strings as the options, and ~preset@id patches that id, or the newest card of that preset when the id is from an earlier reply. Both rules are in the spec (YL.md sections 4 and 5), in the web and Swift parsers, and in six new conformance vectors. The honest size of the win on the channel eval: Sonnet 5 went from 79% to 88%, but only one of those cases is the parser. The rest is run-to-run noise.

images.alt: A choose with Camera roll and Drafts buttons, an ask with Yes, send and Not yet, and a card patched to Mon legs, Thu rest

title: The roadmap catches up with the work
body: The roadmap still said work would start Sep 28 and spread across monthly phases to June 2027. Work started Sep 23, and by Sep 24 Phases 0 and 1 had shipped, with half of Phase 2 and the first part of Phase 5. The phases on /roadmap now show real ship dates taken from the board and the git log, and name the card behind every piece of work still to come. Phases that have not shipped carry no date for now: the old month targets stopped meaning anything, and new ones are a decision, not a guess. The MVP list and the phase cards on /progress match the board too. Nothing to screenshot: this is a text change.

title: Answers are still there when you come back
body: A tester answered a few questions in a chat, left, came back, and every button and slider was blank again, as if nothing had been picked. The answers had reached the agent. Only the phone forgot them, because each component kept its answer in memory and nowhere else. Now the chat rebuilds every answer from the thread itself: the choice, the picks, where the slider stopped, the button tapped, a sent form. When a question was answered twice, the newest answer wins. Replies can reuse the same component name, so each answer goes back to the reply that asked it. A tap after coming back counts as a change of answer, the same as before leaving. A new test opens a saved thread with no network and checks all of it. With the fix switched off, that test fails on every one of those components.

title: No page scrolls sideways on a phone
body: Ten pages slid sideways on a phone. Wide tables in the spec, the channel results and every business doc pushed the whole page out, and so did long links, the playground's picker and phone frame, the benchmark tables, and one long install command on Get started. Now a wide table scrolls inside its own box while the page stays put, long links and commands wrap, and the playground fits a 320 point screen. A script loads all 21 pages at 320, 375, 390 and 430 points wide and fails if any of them is wider than the screen. The first version of that script passed everything: a phone browser quietly zooms out to fit a page that is too wide, so the page's own width grew with it. It now measures against the phone's real width.

images.alt: A wide comparison table on a phone, scrolled sideways inside its own box while the page margins stay in place.
The Get started page on a phone, with a long install command wrapping onto three lines instead of running off the screen.

title: Done buttons always do something
body: A tester got a set of photos to pick from, tapped Done, and nothing happened. Two things went wrong on that one screen. Done stayed switched off until you ticked a small circle on a photo, and nothing said so. And the photos drew taller than their row, so they covered Done and took its taps. Now Done always answers, even with nothing picked (the agent hears "None of these"), a line under the photos says to tap the circles, and every photo stays inside its own frame. Multi-pick questions got the same Done fix. New UI tests tap Done slightly off center with and without picks, and they fail on the old build.

title: The site menu works on a phone
body: The header had thirteen links, a GitHub button and a theme switch in one row. On a phone it wrapped into three or four lines of small pills that ate the top of every page, and it wrapped on a laptop too. Now a phone gets the logo, the theme switch and a menu button. The button opens one list with every page, each row a full 44 points tall, and it closes on a tap outside, on Escape, or when you pick a page. On a wide screen the six pages people use most stay in the bar and the rest sit under More. An automated check loads 14 pages at seven widths, from 375 to 1280, and fails if any link wraps, clips, or is smaller than 44 points.

images.alt: yuigui.com on a phone: the header shows the Yui logo, a dark mode button and a round menu button, with the page headline right below.
The phone menu open: a single list of every page, Home through Channel guide and GitHub, each on its own tall row.

title: Every full-screen view now has a way out
body: A tester opened a photo in the gallery, tapped the X, and nothing happened. There was no other way out, so they were stuck. The cause: the X only answered taps on the 22-point glyph itself, up in the corner where a thumb lands short. Now every full-screen view in Yui (photos, zoomed images, storyboards, decks, narrated walkthroughs) has a 44-point X with a larger touch area around it, and a swipe down closes it too. The stage and deck close buttons had the same flaw and got the same fix. Before/after compare can now go full screen as well, keeping its mode and slider, and side by side stacks top and bottom on a tall phone. New UI tests tap slightly off the X's center, swipe down, switch apps and come back, and keep a timer running behind the viewer.

title: The site now leads with what Yui is: a generative user interface
body: The home page used to call Yui a friendly place for your AI agents. That undersold it. Plenty of apps let you text an agent. What Yui does that they do not is let the agent draw the screen. So the headline is now "Meet Yui, a generative user interface." The line under it says what works in the test build today: your agent answers with a timer, a form or a quick choice instead of a wall of text, in a native iPhone app, built for Hermes first. The page title, the link preview card and the README say the same thing. Further down, the who-it-is-for cards now say plainly which parts work today (Hermes) and which are next on the roadmap (other agents, starter agents). The mission did not change.

images.alt: The yuigui.com home page hero: the headline Meet Yui, a generative user interface, a short line about agents drawing timers, forms and choices, and two phone screenshots of a tabata timer in chat, light and dark
The new link preview card: the coral Yui wordmark, the same headline, and a phone showing a tabata timer the agent drew mid-chat

title: Ready for Apple's beta review: a demo agent, help, and a full privacy page
body: Apple's reviewer needs to see Yui work, but a new account has no agent until you connect your own. So the sign-in screen now has a small Demo code link. The code lives only in the review notes, and it opens one shared demo account with an agent called Demo. Demo is scripted, with no AI model behind it and no access to any computer: say hi and it answers with a menu, tap Workout and the next screen asks what gear you have. If the reviewer deletes the demo account, it comes back empty and Demo reconnects within about a minute. Settings has a new Help and feedback section: a help page at yuigui.com/help, the connect guide, and an email link that fills in your app version. The privacy page now lists everything Yui keeps: the computers your agents run on, agent access keys, the counters behind the limits, one day of addresses for wrong pairing codes, and what we declare on Apple's privacy label. Tested live: 21 checks on the demo sign-in and agent, plus a simulator run from the demo code to Settings.

The Demo agent's thread: a greeting and a card asking What should we try? with Workout, Plan dinner, Focus timer, My week and Quick lesson buttons

title: Safe for strangers: limits, an off switch, and 90 days of history
body: Before anyone outside can install Yui, the backend has to hold up against people we don't know. Yui now has limits on how fast an account can send and how fast an agent's computer can answer, sized so a phone that was offline or a Mac that slept can still catch up in one go. A refused message is not lost: the app and the agent's computer keep it and try again a little later. There are also caps on message size, pictures per day, agents, connected computers and phones per account. We can switch off one account or one computer at once if it misbehaves, without deleting anything, and switch it back on. Messages older than 90 days are now deleted automatically. We tested it with two strangers' accounts trying to read, write, edit, delete and upload into each other's threads and reach anything outside Yui's own tables: 85 live checks, all passing. Nothing to see in the app for this one, it is all on the server. The full limits table is in the app repo's README.

title: Nothing gets lost: sleeping Macs, dropped networks, killed apps
body: Your agent lives on a computer, and computers sleep. Now Yui holds on to every message both ways until it can be delivered, then delivers it once, in order. On the phone, a message goes to a small outbox on the device before it is sent. If the network is gone it stays there, dimmed, with one quiet line saying it goes the moment you're back online, even if you close the app. On the agent's computer, Yui only marks a message done when the agent has finished answering it. If the computer crashes mid-answer, the message is picked up again when it comes back, and an answer that already went out is never sent twice. Replies that can't get out wait on the computer and follow in order. The app also tells the truth about where your agent is: online, asleep (its computer went quiet, with when it was last seen), or offline (its gateway was stopped). We tested it by killing the agent mid-answer, cutting its network while it replied, and killing the app with unsent messages on a simulator. Every message arrived exactly once. A real airplane-mode test on a phone is next, on TestFlight.

images.alt: Two messages sent with no network, shown dimmed, with the line: Not sent yet. It goes the moment you're back online.
Dark mode thread after the network came back: the two messages were delivered once each and the agent answered both in one reply.

title: First run: from sign in to your agent's first screen
body: A new Yui account has no agents, and the app used to hide that behind a friendly greeting that could not actually answer. Now it says so plainly: "Let's connect your first agent", three short steps and one button. Tapping it names the agent and shows the three commands to run on your computer (install the plugin, pair with the code, restart the gateway), with the code already filled in and a copy button on each. If nothing happens after a couple of minutes, or the code runs out, a small card says exactly what to check. The moment your computer connects, the screen flips to connected with a Say hi button that drops you into the new thread. Yui also waits to ask about notifications until you have an agent that could send one. We tested the whole path on a simulator with a fresh throwaway account, in light and dark, playing the computer's side from a script: first screen, code, pairing, hello, and the agent's first screen back.

title: A buzz when your agent answers
body: When an agent answers and Yui is closed, your phone now gets a notification, and tapping it opens that agent's thread with the answer already on screen, even if the app was fully closed. While you are reading a thread, its answers just appear there without buzzing a second time: the open app tells the server which thread is on screen, and a closed app stops counting as open within 90 seconds. Each agent has a Notifications switch in its settings, so a chatty agent can stay quiet and let its answers wait. We tested it on a simulator with real Apple push notifications: an answer in the open thread sent no push, then with the app closed another agent answered, the banner arrived, and the tap landed in the right thread.

title: Connect your agent in three steps
body: Any Hermes agent can now join Yui with one install command, on a Mac or on Linux. Get a pairing code in the app, run hermes plugins install postscarcityai/yui/hermes-plugin/yui --enable, then hermes yui pair with the code and restart the gateway. The new Get started page at yuigui.com/start walks through it. We tested the whole path in an empty Linux container: installing Hermes, the plugin, pairing and the first answer in the app took 86 seconds, and the Yui part (code to answer) took 35. The plugin now works on Hermes's default profile, names Linux machines properly, and prints the next step after each command.

images.alt: yuigui.com Get started page: three numbered steps, get a pairing code, install the Yui plugin, pair and restart the gateway, each command with a copy button.
Yui app: an agent running on a fresh Linux machine answers Hello! Good to see you, then a Tea or coffee? card with two buttons.

title: Every preset, native on iPhone
body: The iPhone app now draws the media, data and learning presets itself, in SwiftUI, instead of leaving them to the web. That is sixteen new ones: gallery in four layouts, compare with a slider, side by side or toggle, storyboard with comments and reordering, image edit, chart, stat, table, card, math, step, calc, deck, page, plan, project and narrate. Math is typeset natively with SwiftMath, charts use Swift Charts, and narrate reads aloud on the phone with the system voice. Decks and the 3D gallery open full screen. Every preset follows the agent's style, so an agent that likes bar charts or a grid gallery gets them without asking. The Swift parser now passes all 323 conformance vectors, the same ones the web renderer passes, and four UI tests tap through every new preset and check what goes back to the agent.

title: Pictures in, photos out
body: Agents can now show you pictures and videos in Yui, and you can send them photos. When an agent makes an image (a storyboard frame, a slide, an edit), it just puts the file or the link in its reply. Yui uploads it to private storage and sends your phone a link that only works for you and expires. Old threads keep their pictures because the app renews the link. When an agent asks for a photo, you take one or pick one from your library, and it arrives on the agent's machine as a file it can open and look at. Hermes agents can render and send a picture in one step with `hermes yui media`. Every photo and picture is deleted with your account, and a daily sweep clears anything no message points at. We tested the locks too: 49 checks that strangers, other accounts and even a revoked agent host cannot read or write your media.

images.alt: Yui app: an agent's reply with a rendered storyboard frame, a coral mug on a sunny kitchen table, captioned Frame 1.
Yui app: the agent asks Snap something for me; the chosen photo of hands shaping a bowl on a pottery wheel shows with Photo sent.

title: The channel guide, now tested
body: Every agent on the Yui channel gets a short guide with each turn: how to put buttons, lists, timers and charts on your screen, and when to just answer in words. We now test that guide. 34 real-life messages (a leg day, a grocery list, a booking, a plain question, a request for a password) go to an agent with the guide, and a script checks every reply with the real Yui Lines parser. The first draft scored 74%. The test caught two bugs no one had seen. The guide taught a way to update a screen that the app actually throws away. And agents often wrote answer options in a way that parses fine but leaves nothing to tap. The rewrite scores 97% and is 20% shorter. It is live for every agent now, and you can read it, with the scores, at yuigui.com/channel. Nothing visual in this one: it is a text guide and a test script.

title: Change your answer
body: Tapped the wrong option? Tap another one. Single choice, multiple choice, yes/no buttons and sliders now stay live after you answer. Your choice stays marked, and a new tap changes it. For multiple choice, change your picks and the button reads Done again; send it and the agent gets the new list. Every change goes back to the agent marked as changed, and the newest answer wins, so the agent adjusts instead of arguing. When an answer really is final, say a booking just got confirmed, the agent can lock it with one line, ~choose +lock, and the buttons stop responding. The playground has it too: pick "Demo: change your answer", tap around, and watch the wire log.

title: Full screen when it matters
body: Some moments deserve the whole phone. An agent can now put a screen over the chat with one line, >full, and bring the chat back with close. Timers, the camera, voice notes and decks open full screen on their own, and a workout always does: start a tabata and it fills the phone, big ring, big buttons. Swipe down or tap the X and you are back in the chat, right where you were. The timer keeps running and shows as a small pill with the time and round, and tapping the pill brings the full screen back. Each agent decides how much it likes this: a coach can put everything full screen, a quieter agent keeps things in the chat and only goes big for workouts. It wears the agent's own look in light and dark. The playground on the site has it too: pick "Demo: full screen" and swipe the stage away.

title: Every agent has its own look
body: In most chat apps every agent looks the same. In Yui the whole app now changes to match the agent you are talking to: background, bubbles, accent color, corner shape, type and motion, in light and dark. A coach agent can be orange with square corners, a wizard violet and serif. A new agent gets its own look on day one, picked from its name, and your agent list shows each one in its colors. Agents can restyle themselves: ask for "more autumn" and the agent sends one line, theme autumn, and the app changes while you watch. Agents can also say which screens they like (full screen, stacked buttons, a gallery style), and Yui tells them that every turn. There is one rule an agent cannot break: every look is checked for readable contrast in light and dark, so no theme can make text hard to read. You can also pick a look yourself in the agent's settings.

title: A plan for every agent framework
body: Yui talks to Hermes today. The goal is any agent, so we mapped how each framework would get in: OpenClaw, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta's Muse Spark, local models through Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM, Flue on Cloudflare, LangGraph, CrewAI, Microsoft's Agent Framework and n8n. The good news: there are only five ways in (a plugin, a hosted connector, a model connector, an MCP server and a webhook), so five pieces of code cover the whole list. Every framework now has a card on the board, and the plan is on the roadmap. None of it starts before the MVP ships. This one is a plan, so there is nothing to screenshot yet.

title: Every page points to the code and the beta
body: The site now ends every page the same way: three ways in. Get the TestFlight beta, star the code on GitHub, or join the waitlist. The public beta is waiting on Apple's review, so for now that card says so and points to the waitlist; the button appears the day Apple says yes. The beta is bring your own agent: you need Hermes running on your own computer. Both repos are open source under Apache 2.0, and GitHub is now in the menu and the footer too. We also made a list of tagged links for social posts, so we can see which posts bring people here. No new tracking was added: the site already had Google Analytics, and a button click now counts as an event there.

title: Pick it up in Yui
body: Any agent can now hand you something from another channel in one step. Say "send it to Yui" (or type /yui) while talking to an agent on Telegram, and it puts what you were working on into Yui as a screen, not a wall of text. Your phone gets a notification, "Urza has something for you in Yui", and tapping it opens the thread with the buttons ready. Every agent reply now pushes too, except for the thread you already have open. It works even for an agent you have not added to Yui yet: its handoff lands in your main agent's thread with its name on it. Tested end to end on the simulator with a real push from Apple. title: Who Yui is on each platform
body: Yui will be @yuiguiai everywhere, and we checked: the name is free on X, Instagram, Threads, TikTok, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit and GitHub (Product Hunt blocked our check). For each account we wrote the bio, the voice, what it posts and why someone would follow it, plus ten example posts that show the voice. Every example is a draft; nothing has been posted and Chris creates the accounts. Avatars and banners use the coral wordmark on cream. Read it at yuigui.com/business/biz-5-social-accounts.

title: Decks, plan mode and narrated walkthroughs
body: Three new kinds of screen. A deck is a presentation: the agent sends one line per slide, with a picture, a few words and speaker notes, and you swipe through it or go full screen. Put a question at the end with the right answer and it becomes a quiz that tells you why. Plan mode turns a string of questions into steps with a progress bar, Back and Next, and a review screen, and the agent gets all your answers at once, as a project it can bring back later with one tap. Narrate has the agent talk you through something while it shows it: a lesson deck page by page, or a website update, before and after, one change at a time, with the words lighting up as they are spoken. Each agent can have its own voice. Try them in the playground: ?demo=deck-lesson, plan-website and narrate-site. The images in the vaccine lesson were generated for it, and the site in the walkthrough is a made-up pottery studio.

title: The board is public
body: You can now watch us work. yuigui.com/board shows every Yui card in four columns: backlog, up next, building, and what shipped in the last 30 days. It comes straight from the kanban board our agents use, so when an agent picks up a card or finishes one, the page follows within half an hour. Shipped cards link to their entry in this log. The MVP bar now counts itself from the same board, and it just moved to 11 of 21. Only titles and short summaries go out. A script checks every export for private details before anything is published, and refuses to write the file if it finds one.

images.alt: The yuigui.com board: backlog, up next, building and shipped columns of Yui cards, with the MVP bar above

title: A content plan, built from what ships
body: How Yui will show up online: every post starts from a line in this log and the screenshot or clip that proves it, so nothing gets written about work that hasn't shipped. It borrows from a blog our agents already run every day: one source, an agent that drafts, a script that rejects bad copy before anyone sees it, and posts scheduled a week ahead. Chris approves every social post. The plan covers four kinds of content (ship posts, this weekly update, longer pieces, short demo clips), what goes on which platform, a six-week calendar and the automation we'd build. Read it at yuigui.com/business/biz-4-content-plan.

title: The MVP, and a bar that shows how close it is
body: Chris asked us not to lose focus, so the roadmap now opens with the MVP: the smallest Yui a stranger can use. Someone who already runs Hermes installs Yui from a public TestFlight link, signs in with Apple, connects their own agents in a few minutes, gets screens and pushes back, and can delete their account from inside the app. That is 21 cards. 10 have shipped, 1 is being built, and the last one is a real outside tester doing the whole path with a stopwatch. The bar on the home page and the roadmap counts them; once the live board lands it will update itself. Everything else went into a deep backlog of 30-odd parked ideas, from a lock-screen timer and group threads to an Android prototype and flows written in Mermaid, so there is always a next card but never a distraction.

images.alt: The MVP progress bar on the yuigui.com roadmap: 48 percent shipped, 10 of 21 cards, with the cards still to go

title: How we will find our first users
body: The outreach plan is public at yuigui.com/business. Hermes users come first, and we found where they gather: the official plugin catalog, a Discord channel the Hermes team names for sharing plugins, and a few dozen builders whose projects sit right next to ours. The plan lists 39 places by name, drafts a message for each kind of place, and sets a pace of two new posts a week at most. Nothing has been sent. Every message waits for Chris to approve it, and nothing goes out at all until a stranger can install the plugin and see a screen from their own agent without help. One honest correction from the research: native agent-drawn screens are not ours alone anymore, since the A2UI project now has a SwiftUI renderer. What we can say is that Yui is a finished iPhone app where Hermes agents draw native screens today.

title: Talk to your agent in Yui
body: Yui is now a messaging platform for Hermes, next to Telegram. Each agent you add gets its own thread in the app and keeps one memory across both, so what you tell it on Telegram it still knows in Yui. Replies can carry Yui Lines, and the app draws them as buttons, pickers, forms and timers; ask for intervals and you get a running timer, not a paragraph. Your taps go back to the agent as short lines like "[yui] n1 ask answer=Yes", and it keeps going from there. The agent's computer dials out, so it opens no ports, and it gets a key that can only read and answer the threads of its own agents. Remove the computer in the app and it is cut off at once. We tested that, and 37 other rules, against the live backend. Every agent also gets the same short guide to the channel on each turn, and agents that don't run Hermes can fetch it too. How it works: spec/RELAY.md.

title: The site now looks like the app
body: yuigui.com wears the same clothes as the iPhone app now. Cream paper, soft plum ink, the coral wordmark up top, rounded type, pastel accents. The colors come straight from the app's theme file, so when the app changes, the site can follow. Light is the default and the moon button in the corner switches to dark. The home page tells the story in plain words: what Yui is, who it is for (people who already run agents, Hermes first), and real screenshots from the current test build. The icon and the link preview use the wordmark too. We also fixed contrast across the site. Every page but the playground now scores 100 on Google's accessibility check, and the playground's last few fixes are queued.

images.alt: The new yuigui.com home page in light mode
Before the rebrand: the old dark site

title: Business docs, in the open
body: The business side of Yui is now public at yuigui.com/business. Two docs so far. A marketing and positioning brief: who Yui is for first (people already running Hermes agents), how we will launch (private beta, open source, Show HN, then the App Store) and what we will measure. And a revenue plan with the rules we hold ourselves to: free and open source for anyone who brings their own agent, no dark patterns, charge only where we carry a cost. The research was humbling. Phone apps for self-hosted agents already exist, and OpenClaw's own app lets agents draw widgets, in a web view. What nobody ships yet is native screens drawn by your agent, and no Hermes agent can draw a screen at all. That is where Yui starts. The competitor notes are published too, sources and all.

title: Yui is open source
body: Both repos are public now, under the Apache-2.0 license. postscarcityai/yuigui holds the Yui Lines spec, the test cases every parser must pass, the reference parser and this site. postscarcityai/yui holds the iPhone app, the Swift parser, the backend and the Hermes plugin. Before flipping them we scanned every commit in both repos for keys and tokens and found none. The one key in the app is a public client key that can't read anyone's data. Each repo now has a README with screenshots, a guide for contributors, a code of conduct and a private way to report security problems. A good place to start: write a Yui Lines parser in a language we don't have yet.

title: Yui Lines learn charts, equations and experiments
body: Agents can now show numbers and teach with them, one line each. chart draws line, bar, area, scatter, pie and donut charts from data written right in the line, with more series, stacking and error bars (write 12.5±0.4), or from a live table on the same screen, so when the table changes the chart redraws. Every chart has a Table view and follows the app's light or dark theme; each theme has its own set of chart colors, checked so people with color blindness can tell the series apart. stat is one big number with its change and a small trend line, and tapping lb or °C shows kg or °F. math typesets equations. step walks through a derivation or a lab protocol one step at a time, with optional timers. calc turns a formula into sliders that redraw a chart as you drag: slide the launch angle and watch the range peak at 45 degrees. Tables can now be sorted and carry units. 53 new test cases pin the syntax, 251 in all. The app picks these up next.

title: Your agents are yours to add
body: Chris's next piece of feedback: agents are added by you, not baked into the app. So the Urza and Arnold placeholders are gone. The agents screen now starts empty with an Add your first agent button, and each agent shows its avatar, an online or offline dot and when it was last seen. You can rename, recolor, reorder, pick a default or remove one (which also deletes that conversation). There are three ways to add one, and all land in the same place. In the app: name it, get a 6-digit code, type one command on the computer it runs on. From that computer: once it is paired, any other agent on it can join with one command and no code. Or ask an agent: Settings has an Agent access token you can hand to one of your agents so it can add and manage agents for you. That token can't read your messages, and 59 new automated checks try to make it. For testing, one agent is set up: Yui itself. Build 14 is on TestFlight.

title: Yui Lines learn pictures and video
body: Agents can now show media, not just describe it. Four new one-line presets: gallery (photos and clips as a swipe row, a vertical feed, a 3D coverflow stack or a grid, with tap to go full screen and an optional pick-your-favorites mode), video, compare (before and after with a drag slider, side by side or tap to toggle, plus numbered boxes where the agent points at what changed) and storyboard (ordered frames you can reorder and comment on, or a script with no pictures yet). An image can also be marked up: circle the part you want changed, type what you want, and the agent gets the area and the instruction, runs the edit and answers with a before and after. Every demo on the playground uses images we generated for it. 33 new test cases pin the syntax, 198 in all. The app picks these up next.

A gallery photo opened full screen

title: Beta feedback: the debug screen is gone
body: First real TestFlight feedback, from Chris: the Paste YL screen had to go. It was a developer tool that showed the raw lines agents write, parse counts and event data, and no one using Yui should ever see that. Yui Lines stay under the hood. The button it lived behind now opens Your agents: Yui is there today, and Urza and Arnold wait with a Connect Hermes to start note until the Hermes channel lands. How to use Yui is something the agents learn at the start of every chat, not something you read. Build 13 is on TestFlight.

title: Accounts: Sign in with Apple, and delete it in the app
body: Yui now has accounts. You sign in with Apple, no password, and Settings has a Delete account button that wipes everything Yui stores for you and removes Yui from your Apple ID. The App Store requires that, and it is the right default anyway. The server side is locked down on purpose: Yui accounts get their own database role that can only see Yui's own tables, and each account only its own rows. 63 automated checks try to break that, including one that creates a test account, fills every table, deletes it, and counts zero rows left. Plain-language privacy page at yuigui.com/privacy.

title: Yui drops the cat
body: The round cat is gone. Chris noticed the hand-drawn Yui wordmark already looks like a cat, abstractly: the bunny-ear arms on the Y read as ears. So the logo is the face now. Yui's own avatar in chat is that Y on its own, in coral. Each agent gets a small pastel chip with its first letter in heavy rounded type, colored from the theme file, so when agents get their own looks their chips change with them. The empty chat screen and settings show the wordmark with a few warm words, no drawing. Build 10 is on TestFlight.

images.alt: The empty chat after the cat was dropped: just the coral wordmark, dark theme
A chat with a timer card and no mascot

title: Yui draws its first six screens
body: An agent can now reply with a timer, a question, a multiple choice, a pick-several, a form or a list, and Yui draws it as a real card inside the chat instead of plain text. The timer counts rounds on a ring and beeps on the last three seconds. Forms handle text, numbers, dates, sliders, yes/no toggles and voice notes, and will not submit until the required fields are filled. Every tap goes back to the agent as one small event, and your answer shows up as your own chat bubble. All the styling comes from the same theme file, so a restyle changes these cards too. A hidden paste box lets us test any Yui Lines reply by hand. Build 9 is on TestFlight.

images.alt: A choose screen in chat: which split today, push, pull or legs
A Tabata timer card counting down in chat, dark theme
A daily check-in form with a mood slider, switches and notes

title: The wordmark moves into the app
body: Chris's hand-drawn Yui wordmark, the one with bunny-ear arms on the Y, now sits in the app's top bar, on the empty chat screen and in settings. Its coral is now the app's main color too: the send button, your chat bubbles and the selected toggle all use it, with the pastels kept for the smaller touches. The coral is stored in the same theme file as everything else, so an agent that restyles the app recolors the logo along with it. It reads clearly on both the cream light mode and the dark plum mode, so one logo file covers both. Yui the cat stays as the face of the agent. Build 8 is on TestFlight.

A chat with the wordmark in the top bar

title: Yui Lines has a test suite
body: Yui Lines is the one-line format an agent uses to put a timer or a question on your screen. It now has a shared test suite: 165 small cases, each a bit of input plus the exact result a parser must return. The web playground's parser and the new Swift parser inside the app both pass every case, and any future parser, Android included, has to pass the same files. Writing the cases turned up a few gaps in the spec, such as what a mistyped form field should do. Those answers are now written down.

title: Yui gets a face
body: Yui now has a look: a round white cat named Yui, soft pastels on warm cream paper, rounded type, and a little bounce when you tap send. The feel borrows from Korean character apps like Kakao Friends: cute, but not childish. There is a light and dark mode with a toggle in settings. Under the hood every color, corner and animation lives in one small data file, so later an agent can restyle the whole app on the fly. Build 5 is on TestFlight with the new icon.

title: First TestFlight build
body: The Swift app exists. Build 4 is a bare SwiftUI chat screen with a placeholder icon, signed and uploaded to TestFlight straight from the build machine with no one opening Xcode. It does nothing useful yet. What matters is the pipeline: from here every change can reach a phone in minutes. First upload was rejected for a missing app icon, fixed in one commit.

title: Waitlist open
body: The waitlist is live on yuigui.com. Sign up for TestFlight invites and occasional updates. Signups land in a small table in PostScarcity AI's existing database, no new infrastructure.

title: Apple Developer account active
body: Yui has an Apple Developer account, so TestFlight is unblocked. Xcode is installing on the build machine. Next: the Swift project and an automatic TestFlight build on every push.

title: yuigui.com is live
body: The hub now lives at yuigui.com. Yui is built in public: this log updates as work ships, and a weekly update lands every Friday.

title: Stack decision: all Swift
body: Yui will be a native SwiftUI iPhone app, not React Native. The reason is the product: Yui should feel like part of the phone, and the features that set it apart (a workout timer on the lock screen, Siri and the Action button, Apple's on-device model and speech) are native Apple surfaces. The preset design keeps the app small, so an Android port later is a port of the presets, not a rewrite. No Apple Watch app yet. Yui Lines stays platform-neutral: the web playground and the Swift app parse it the same way.

title: Source on GitHub
body: The hub, roadmap, Yui Lines spec and benchmark now live at postscarcityai/yuigui. The app code gets its own repo, yui.

title: Yui Lines v0: spec, 12 presets, playground, token benchmark
body: Agents now speak Yui Lines: one short line per component, no UI code, no JSON. Spec at /yl, live playground at /playground with all 12 presets (timer, ask, choose, pick, slide, form, list, table, card, image, camera, mic), line-by-line streaming, ~patch, >screen routing, save/show and the custom {json} escape hatch. Benchmark on 10 screens with real tokenizers: YL is 1.6x smaller than minified JSON, 2.7x smaller than pretty JSON, 3.9x smaller than a component-tree document.
